The team finishing last without a single win is said to have taken the wooden spoon.

question: In which year did England win the Rugby World Cup?
explanation: England won the Rugby World Cup in 2003, defeating Australia in the final in Sydney with a drop goal by Jonny Wilkinson in the last minute of extra time. It remains the only occasion on which a northern hemisphere team has won the tournament. The team was captained by Martin Johnson, and the players received a rapturous welcome home. England had reached the final in 1991 and did so again in 2007 and 2019 without winning. Rugby union has two distinct codes in Britain, with rugby league, played with thirteen players, strongest in the north of England. Wilkinson struck the winning kick with his weaker right foot, seconds from the end.

question: What is the difference between rugby union and rugby league?
option_a: They are separate codes with different rules and team sizes
option_b: They are the same sport under two names
option_c: League is played only by amateurs and union only by professionals
option_d: League is played with a round ball and union with an oval one
explanation: Rugby union and rugby league are distinct sports that separated in 1895 over the question of paying players for time off work. Union is played with fifteen players a side and league with thirteen, and they differ in the rules governing tackles, scrums, line-outs and scoring. Rugby league is strongest in the north of England, particularly Yorkshire and Lancashire, with the Super League as its top competition and the Challenge Cup as its knockout tournament, while union is played throughout the United Kingdom and is especially prominent in Wales, Scotland and the Irish provinces. Both have their own international competitions.

question: Who was the first person to run a mile in under four minutes?
option_a: Sebastian Coe
option_b: Sir Roger Bannister
option_c: Sir Mo Farah
option_d: Daley Thompson
explanation: Sir Roger Bannister, then a medical student, ran a mile in under four minutes at the Iffley Road track in Oxford in May 1954, a feat many had believed to be beyond human capability. He was assisted by pacemakers and achieved a time of three minutes and fifty-nine and four tenths seconds. He went on to become a distinguished neurologist. Sebastian Coe was an Olympic middle-distance champion in the 1980s who later chaired the organising committee for the London Olympic Games, Daley Thompson won Olympic decathlon titles, and Sir Mo Farah won multiple Olympic distance titles. The record has since been lowered by well over fifteen seconds by later runners.

question: Which British athlete won Olympic gold medals at five consecutive Games in rowing?
option_a: Sir Steve Redgrave
option_b: Sir Mo Farah
option_c: Sir Chris Hoy
option_d: Sir Bradley Wiggins
explanation: Sir Steve Redgrave won rowing gold medals at five consecutive Olympic Games between 1984 and 2000, an achievement without parallel in an endurance sport and all the more remarkable because he was diagnosed with diabetes during that period. He was partnered in later years by Matthew Pinsent, who won four golds of his own. Sir Chris Hoy won six Olympic cycling golds across several Games, Sir Bradley Wiggins won the Tour de France in 2012 and multiple Olympic titles on both track and road, and Sir Mo Farah won the five thousand and ten thousand metres at two Games. He was voted BBC Sports Personality of the Year after his final victory in Sydney.

question: Which British cyclist won the Tour de France in 2012?
option_a: Laura Kenny
option_b: Mark Cavendish
option_c: Sir Bradley Wiggins
option_d: Sir Chris Hoy
explanation: Sir Bradley Wiggins became the first British rider to win the Tour de France in 2012, and days later won an Olympic time trial gold medal at the London Games. Other British riders have since won the Tour, and the country has become a leading force in cycling. Sir Chris Hoy, from Edinburgh, won six Olympic gold medals on the track, Mark Cavendish has won a record-equalling number of stages of the Tour de France as a sprinter, and Dame Laura Kenny is Britain's most successful female Olympian, with multiple track cycling gold medals. British riders have since won the race several more times, a remarkable change of fortunes.

question: Which annual horse race is run at Aintree near Liverpool?
option_a: The Grand National
option_b: Royal Ascot
option_c: The Cheltenham Gold Cup
option_d: The Derby
explanation: The Grand National is a steeplechase run each spring at Aintree racecourse near Liverpool over a long course with large fences, including the famous Becher's Brook, and it is watched by an enormous television audience. Many people who never otherwise bet place a wager on it, often through office sweepstakes. The Derby is a flat race run at Epsom in June, Royal Ascot is a meeting in Berkshire attended by the royal family and known for its dress code and hats, and the Cheltenham Gold Cup is the leading race of the National Hunt festival in March. Around forty horses start, and the course is run over more than four miles with thirty fences.

question: What is the Boat Race?
option_a: A canoe race on the River Severn
option_b: A sailing regatta held at Cowes
option_c: An annual rowing contest between Oxford and Cambridge universities on the Thames
option_d: A powerboat competition on Lake Windermere
explanation: The Boat Race is an annual rowing contest between crews from Oxford and Cambridge universities, rowed over a four and a quarter mile course on the Thames in west London between Putney and Mortlake. It was first held in 1829 and is watched by large crowds along the riverbank and by a television audience. Women's crews now race on the same day and over the same course. Cowes Week on the Isle of Wight is the best known British sailing regatta, and Henley Royal Regatta is a major rowing event held on the Thames in Oxfordshire each summer. The losing crew traditionally has the right to challenge the winners to a rematch the following year.

question: Where was golf first developed?
option_a: Wales
option_b: England
option_c: Ireland
option_d: Scotland
explanation: Golf developed in Scotland, where it has been played for centuries, and the Old Course at St Andrews in Fife is regarded as the home of the game. The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews was long responsible for the rules, and the Open Championship, the oldest of golf's major tournaments, is played each year on a links course in Britain, rotating among a small group of venues. Scotland has an exceptional concentration of historic courses, and golf is played throughout the United Kingdom at thousands of clubs and public courses. Records of the game in Scotland go back at least to the fifteenth century, when it was briefly banned.

question: What is the Open Championship?
option_a: A snooker competition held in Sheffield
option_b: A tennis tournament held at Queen's Club
option_c: An athletics meeting open to amateurs
option_d: The oldest of golf's major tournaments, played on British links courses
explanation: The Open Championship, often called simply the Open, was first played in 1860 and is the oldest of the four major championships in golf. It is held each July on one of a rotation of links courses around the coasts of Scotland, England and Northern Ireland, including St Andrews, Carnoustie, Royal Birkdale and Royal Portrush. The winner receives the Claret Jug. Unpredictable coastal weather is part of its character. The World Snooker Championship is held each spring at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield, and the Queen's Club tournament precedes Wimbledon in the tennis calendar. Players must contend with deep bunkers, firm fairways and coastal wind quite unlike inland courses.

question: Where is the World Snooker Championship held each year?
option_a: The NEC in Birmingham
option_b: The Crucible Theatre in Sheffield
option_c: The SSE Hydro in Glasgow
option_d: Wembley Arena in London
explanation: The World Snooker Championship has been staged at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield since 1977 and is the sport's most prestigious tournament, played over more than two weeks each spring with matches over many frames. The venue is unusually small and intimate for a major sporting event, with the audience very close to the table. Snooker became enormously popular in Britain with the spread of colour television, and a famously late final in 1985 drew a huge audience. Darts, another sport with strong British followings, holds its leading championship in north London each winter. The final is played over two days, with the winner needing eighteen frames.

question: Which British driver has won multiple Formula One world championships in recent decades?
option_a: Graham Hill
option_b: Nigel Mansell
option_c: Lewis Hamilton
option_d: Jackie Stewart
explanation: Lewis Hamilton has won seven Formula One world drivers' championships, equalling the all-time record, and holds records for race victories and pole positions. Britain has a long and successful history in motor racing: Sir Jackie Stewart won three world titles in the 1960s and 1970s and campaigned vigorously for improved safety, Graham Hill and his son Damon Hill both won the championship, and Nigel Mansell won it in 1992. The British Grand Prix is held at Silverstone, and a large proportion of Formula One teams are based in England. Hamilton began in karting and came through a junior driver programme before reaching Formula One. Britain has produced more world champions than any other country.

question: Which British sailor became famous for solo round-the-world sailing?
option_a: Dame Ellen MacArthur
option_b: Dame Sarah Storey
option_c: Dame Kelly Holmes
option_d: Dame Tanni Grey-Thompson
explanation: Dame Ellen MacArthur set a record in 2005 for the fastest solo circumnavigation of the globe, sailing single-handed in a large trimaran and enduring extreme conditions with very little sleep. She later retired from competitive sailing to found a charitable foundation promoting the circular economy. Dame Kelly Holmes won Olympic gold medals at eight hundred and fifteen hundred metres in 2004, Dame Tanni Grey-Thompson won numerous Paralympic titles in wheelchair racing, and Dame Sarah Storey is Britain's most decorated Paralympian, competing in both swimming and cycling. Her voyage lasted just over seventy-one days, and she was made a dame while still at sea. Solo ocean racing demands navigation, sail repair and endurance from a single person.

question: Where did the Paralympic Games originate?
option_a: In Australia after the Second World War
option_b: At the Olympic stadium in Athens
option_c: At the University of Oxford
option_d: At Stoke Mandeville Hospital in Buckinghamshire
explanation: The Paralympic movement traces its origins to sporting competitions organised for patients with spinal injuries at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in Buckinghamshire by Dr Ludwig Guttmann, a refugee from Nazi Germany, beginning in 1948 to coincide with the London Olympics. These games grew into an international event and eventually into the Paralympic Games, now held alongside the Olympics in the same host city. The London Games of 2012 attracted record crowds and television audiences for Paralympic sport, and British Paralympians have been among the most successful in the world. Guttmann believed sport was essential to the rehabilitation of patients with spinal injuries. The hospital still hosts a national centre for disability sport today.

question: Which British athlete won gold in both the 800 metres and the 1500 metres at the 2004 Olympics?
option_a: Dame Kelly Holmes
option_b: Jessica Ennis-Hill
option_c: Paula Radcliffe
option_d: Denise Lewis
explanation: Dame Kelly Holmes won the eight hundred metres and the fifteen hundred metres at the Athens Olympics of 2004, a rare double achieved after a career repeatedly interrupted by injury, and her expression of disbelief as she crossed the line became one of the enduring images of British sport. Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill won the heptathlon at the London Games of 2012, Denise Lewis had won the same event in 2000, and Paula Radcliffe set a world record in the marathon that stood for many years. Britain has a strong tradition in middle-distance running. She had served in the British Army before becoming a full-time athlete. Her second victory came by the narrowest of margins on the line.

question: Which British distance runner won Olympic gold in both the 5,000 and 10,000 metres?
option_a: Sir Roger Bannister
option_b: Sir Steve Redgrave
option_c: Sir Mo Farah
option_d: Sir Chris Hoy
explanation: Sir Mo Farah won the five thousand and ten thousand metres at both the London Olympics of 2012 and the Rio Games of 2016, a feat achieved by very few athletes, and he added multiple world championship titles. Born in Somalia, he came to Britain as a child and became one of the country's most successful track athletes before moving to road running. His victories on what became known as Super Saturday at the London Games, alongside those of Jessica Ennis-Hill and Greg Rutherford, are among the most celebrated moments in recent British sport. His victory celebration, forming an M above his head, became widely imitated. He was knighted for his services to athletics.

question: What is the FA Cup?
option_a: A league competition for the top twenty clubs only
option_b: A competition between the national teams of the four nations
option_c: A trophy awarded to the best player of the season
option_d: A knockout football competition open to clubs from many levels of the game
explanation: The Football Association Challenge Cup, universally called the FA Cup, is the oldest football competition in the world, first played in the 1870s. It is a knockout tournament in which hundreds of clubs take part, from small amateur sides in the early rounds through to the leading professional teams, which is why it regularly produces upsets known as giant-killings. The final is played at Wembley Stadium each May. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own cup competitions, and the Premier League is the top division of the English league system. Winning the cup also brings entry to a European club competition the following season. The trophy itself has been remade several times since the 1870s.

question: What is the Premier League?
option_a: The leading rugby league competition
option_b: A cricket tournament played in the summer
option_c: The top division of professional football in England
option_d: The governing body of British athletics
explanation: The Premier League is the highest division of the English football league system, formed in 1992 when the leading clubs broke away to negotiate their own broadcasting arrangements. It has become one of the wealthiest and most widely watched sports competitions in the world, with matches broadcast to a global audience and players drawn from many countries. Below it sit further divisions with promotion and relegation between them. Scotland has its own professional leagues, and the Super League is the top competition in rugby league, played mainly in the north of England. Twenty clubs compete each season, playing one another home and away. The bottom three are relegated to the division below.

question: Where do England play their home rugby union international matches?
option_a: Wembley
option_b: Twickenham
option_c: The Principality Stadium
option_d: Murrayfield
explanation: Twickenham in south-west London is the home ground of English rugby union and one of the largest dedicated rugby stadiums in the world. Scotland play at Murrayfield in Edinburgh and Wales at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, which has a retractable roof, while Ireland play at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin. Wembley is the national football stadium in London, rebuilt in the 2000s and also used for the FA Cup final, major concerts and rugby league's Challenge Cup final. Each of these grounds hosts matches during the Six Nations Championship. The ground holds over eighty thousand spectators and has a museum of the sport. It was built on land formerly used as a market garden.

question: Which sport is associated with the Wimbledon tradition of eating strawberries and cream?
option_a: Polo
option_b: Tennis
option_c: Rowing
option_d: Cricket
explanation: Strawberries and cream have been associated with the Wimbledon tennis championships for well over a century, and enormous quantities are eaten during the fortnight each summer. Other traditions of the tournament include the strict all-white clothing rule for players, the absence of advertising around the courts, the royal box, and the overnight queue for tickets sold on the day. Play was traditionally suspended on the middle Sunday, though that has changed in recent years, and retractable roofs on the main courts now allow matches to continue during rain. Line judges have in recent years been replaced at many tournaments by electronic systems. The grass courts are re-sown and rested each year after the championships.

question: What is the Ryder Cup?
option_a: A cricket match between England and the West Indies
option_b: A cycling race across France
option_c: A golf competition between teams from Europe and the United States
option_d: A sailing contest held at Cowes
explanation: The Ryder Cup is a golf competition held every two years between a team from Europe and a team from the United States, played alternately on each side of the Atlantic. Unusually for professional golf it is a team event decided by matchplay rather than stroke play, and no prize money is paid, which is often said to explain the unusual intensity and emotion of the occasion. British players have featured prominently throughout its history, and the competition was contested by Great Britain and Ireland before being widened to include continental Europe in 1979. The cup is named after Samuel Ryder, an English seed merchant who donated the trophy. Home crowds are famously partisan, which is unusual for the sport.

question: Which cricket format lasts around three hours and was developed in England?
option_a: First-class county cricket
option_b: Test cricket
option_c: Twenty20
option_d: The Ashes
explanation: Twenty20 cricket, in which each side bats for a maximum of twenty overs, was introduced in England in 2003 to attract new audiences with a game that could be completed in an evening. It proved enormously popular and has spread worldwide, generating major professional competitions and its own World Cup. Test cricket, by contrast, is played over up to five days and is regarded by traditionalists as the game's highest form, while first-class county cricket is played over four days. One-day internationals occupy a middle ground of fifty overs a side. Matches are often played in the evening with music and entertainment between overs. Domestic Twenty20 competitions now exist in many cricketing nations.

question: Which annual award recognises the outstanding British sportsperson of the year?
option_a: The Turner Prize
option_b: The Booker Prize
option_c: The Mercury Prize
option_d: BBC Sports Personality of the Year
explanation: BBC Sports Personality of the Year has been awarded since the 1950s and is decided by a public vote, with the ceremony broadcast in December each year and additional awards made for coach, team, overseas personality and lifetime achievement. The Turner Prize is awarded for contemporary art, the Mercury Prize for an album of the year by a British or Irish act, and the Booker Prize for a work of fiction published in English. Each of these prizes attracts considerable public attention and debate, and they are among the most prominent awards in British cultural life. Past winners include athletes, cyclists, boxers, footballers and drivers from across the sporting spectrum.

question: Which of these sports had its modern rules codified in Britain?
option_a: Judo
option_b: Association football
option_c: Basketball
option_d: Baseball
explanation: A striking number of the world's major sports were given their modern rules in Britain during the nineteenth century, when schools, universities and new clubs sought common codes so that teams could compete against one another. The Football Association was founded in 1863, rugby's governing body followed, lawn tennis was codified in the 1870s, the laws of cricket had long been overseen from Lord's, and golf's rules came from Scotland. British traders, soldiers and engineers then carried these games around the world. Basketball and baseball developed in the United States, and judo originated in Japan. Table tennis, squash, badminton and modern boxing rules also have British origins. The spread of these games followed British trade and empire.

question: How do the four nations of the UK compete in most international sporting events?
option_a: Always as a single United Kingdom team
option_b: Each nation competes only against the others
option_c: Usually as separate teams, though as Team GB at the Olympics
option_d: Only England is permitted to enter
explanation: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland field separate national teams in most sports, including football, rugby union and the Commonwealth Games, a legacy of the games having been organised within each nation before international competition existed. At the Olympic and Paralympic Games, however, athletes compete together as Great Britain and Northern Ireland, generally known as Team GB. Cricket is different again: England and Wales field a combined team, and Ireland fields a single team drawn from both jurisdictions, as it does in rugby union. This arrangement occasionally causes confusion abroad, since the United Kingdom is one state. Football's governing bodies recognise each nation separately for historical reasons. Team GB has entered every modern Olympic Games.

question: Which stadium is the national football stadium of England?
option_a: The Emirates
option_b: Wembley
option_c: Old Trafford
option_d: Anfield
explanation: Wembley Stadium in north-west London is the home of the England football team and the venue for the FA Cup final, the League Cup final and other major matches, as well as concerts and rugby league's Challenge Cup final. The original stadium, with its distinctive twin towers, opened in 1923 and hosted the 1966 World Cup final; it was demolished and replaced by a new stadium with a great arch, opened in 2007. Old Trafford, Anfield and the Emirates are the grounds of individual clubs, in Manchester, Liverpool and London respectively. Its arch is visible across much of London and is lit at night. The stadium holds ninety thousand spectators, the largest in the country.

question: What is Royal Ascot?
option_a: A horse racing meeting in Berkshire attended by the royal family
option_b: A regatta held on the Thames
option_c: A golf tournament played in Scotland
option_d: A motor racing event at Silverstone
explanation: Royal Ascot is a five-day horse racing meeting held each June at Ascot racecourse in Berkshire, close to Windsor. It is attended by members of the royal family, who arrive each afternoon in a carriage procession, and it is known as much for fashion as for racing, with a strict dress code in the Royal Enclosure and elaborate hats much in evidence. Other major fixtures in the racing calendar include the Derby at Epsom, the Grand National at Aintree, the Cheltenham Festival in March and the Scottish Grand National at Ayr. The meeting has been held since 1711, when it was founded by Queen Anne. Gold Cup day is traditionally known as Ladies' Day.

question: Which race is run at Epsom each June?
option_a: The Gold Cup
option_b: The Derby
option_c: The Scottish Grand National
option_d: The Grand National
explanation: The Derby is a flat race for three-year-old horses run at Epsom Downs in Surrey each June and is among the most prestigious races in the world, having been first run in 1780. Its name has been borrowed by sporting contests around the globe, and in Britain a match between two local rival clubs is commonly called a derby. The Grand National at Aintree is a steeplechase over jumps, the Cheltenham Gold Cup is the leading National Hunt race, and the Scottish Grand National is run at Ayr. The race is run over roughly a mile and a half on a demanding undulating course. It forms part of the English Triple Crown of flat racing.

question: What is the Commonwealth Games' distinctive feature for the UK?
option_a: Only Team GB may enter
option_b: Events are held only in London
option_c: Competitors must be amateurs
option_d: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland compete as separate teams
explanation: At the Commonwealth Games, held every four years, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland enter separate teams, as do the Isle of Man, Jersey, Guernsey and several British overseas territories, which is unlike the Olympic Games where athletes compete together as Team GB. The Games include sports such as netball, lawn bowls and squash that do not appear in the Olympic programme, and para-sport events are fully integrated into the main schedule. British cities that have hosted them include Manchester, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Birmingham. The Games are held in the years between successive Olympic Games. More than seventy teams take part, from every inhabited continent. They are sometimes described as the Friendly Games.

question: Which sport is played at the Crucible, Wembley and Twickenham respectively?
option_a: Boxing, rowing and netball
option_b: Snooker, football and rugby union
option_c: Darts, cricket and tennis
option_d: Squash, hockey and golf
explanation: The Crucible Theatre in Sheffield hosts the World Snooker Championship each spring, Wembley Stadium in London is the national football stadium and the venue for the FA Cup final, and Twickenham is the home of English rugby union. Other well known British venues include Lord's and the Oval for cricket, the All England Club at Wimbledon for tennis, Murrayfield and the Principality Stadium for rugby in Scotland and Wales, Silverstone for motor racing, and Aintree, Epsom, Ascot and Cheltenham for horse racing. Sport occupies a prominent place in British national life. Many of these venues also host concerts and events outside the sporting calendar. Sports tourism brings substantial numbers of visitors to Britain each year.

question: What is a common feature of British participation in sport at local level?
option_a: Sport is played only in schools
option_b: Only professional athletes may join a club
option_c: All clubs are funded and run by central government
option_d: Large numbers of amateur clubs and teams run by volunteers
explanation: Sport in Britain rests on a very large base of amateur clubs, leagues and teams, covering football, cricket, rugby, hockey, netball, bowls, running, swimming, cycling and much else, and these are overwhelmingly run by volunteers who coach, organise fixtures, maintain grounds and raise funds. Participation in local sport is one of the ways the official handbook suggests people can take part in community life. Local authorities provide leisure centres, pitches and pools, and national governing bodies and charitable funding support grassroots participation, but the day-to-day work is voluntary. Schools, universities and workplaces also run teams and leagues of their own. Walking, swimming and running are the most widely practised activities overall.

question: Which of these events took place in London in 2012?
option_a: The Commonwealth Games
option_b: The Rugby World Cup final
option_c: The football World Cup
option_d: The Olympic and Paralympic Games
explanation: London hosted the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2012, becoming the first city to stage the Olympics three times after 1908 and 1948. The Games were centred on a new park in Stratford in east London, an area substantially regenerated for the purpose, and Team GB achieved its best modern medal haul, while the Paralympic Games drew record crowds. The opening ceremony, directed by Danny Boyle, presented a history of British life featuring the Industrial Revolution, the National Health Service and British popular music. Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games two years later. The Games were widely judged a success and left a substantial legacy of sporting facilities. Ticket demand was so high that a ballot was used to allocate seats.

question: Which British boxer or boxing feature is part of the country's sporting tradition?
option_a: Boxing is illegal in the United Kingdom
option_b: Amateur and professional boxing clubs exist across the country, with British world champions in many eras
option_c: Professional boxing was abolished in 1945
option_d: Boxing may only be practised in Northern Ireland
explanation: Boxing has a long history in Britain, with rules named after the Marquess of Queensberry codified in the nineteenth century and still underlying the modern sport. Amateur clubs operate in towns and cities across the country, often with a strong role in youth work, and Britain has produced many world champions and Olympic medallists in both the men's and women's divisions. Major professional fights attract large audiences. The sport is regulated by boards of control that oversee medical standards and licensing, and it remains the subject of continuing debate about safety. Women's boxing was included in the Olympic Games for the first time in London in 2012. Britain won its first women's Olympic boxing gold at those Games.

question: What is the significance of Murrayfield?
option_a: It is a golf course in Fife
option_b: It is Scotland's national rugby union stadium in Edinburgh
option_c: It is a horse racing course near Glasgow
option_d: It is the home of Scottish football
explanation: Murrayfield in Edinburgh is the national stadium for rugby union in Scotland and one of the largest sports grounds in the country, hosting Six Nations matches and other internationals as well as concerts. Hampden Park in Glasgow is the national football stadium of Scotland and has hosted cup finals, internationals and, in 2014, athletics at the Commonwealth Games. St Andrews in Fife is the most famous golf course in the world, and Ayr and Musselburgh are well known Scottish racecourses. Each of the four nations has its own sporting institutions and traditions. Before kick-off the crowd traditionally sings 'Flower of Scotland' without accompaniment. The ground has hosted rugby internationals since the 1920s.

question: Which competition is contested for the Calcutta Cup?
option_a: The annual rugby union match between England and Scotland
option_b: A football match between Liverpool and Everton
option_c: A rowing race between Oxford and Cambridge
option_d: A cricket series between England and India
explanation: The Calcutta Cup is awarded to the winner of the annual rugby union match between England and Scotland, played as part of the Six Nations Championship. The trophy was made from melted-down silver rupees when a rugby club in Calcutta was disbanded in the 1870s, and it is among the oldest trophies in international sport. The fixture is one of the oldest rivalries in rugby, first contested in 1871. Other named trophies within the championship include the Millennium Trophy, contested between England and Ireland, and the Centenary Quaich between Scotland and Ireland. Because of its fragility, the trophy that is presented is now usually a replica. The fixture is among the oldest in international sport.

question: Which two British cities are especially associated with major football rivalries?
option_a: Only London has football clubs
option_b: Football is not played in Scotland
option_c: Clubs are not permitted in Wales
option_d: Manchester, Liverpool, Glasgow and London all have long-standing club rivalries
explanation: Intense local football rivalries are a feature of British sporting life. Manchester has United and City, Liverpool has Liverpool and Everton, Glasgow has Celtic and Rangers, whose rivalry also carries historic religious and cultural dimensions, and London has many clubs including Arsenal, Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and West Ham United. Matches between local rivals are known as derbies. Welsh clubs including Cardiff City and Swansea City play within the English league structure, while Wales also has its own domestic league, and Northern Ireland has its own league as well. Match days bring very large crowds into city centres and onto public transport. Supporters' loyalties are often inherited within families across generations.

question: What is the role of volunteers at major British sporting events?
option_a: They help run events, as the 'Games Makers' did at the 2012 Olympics
option_b: They are appointed by the government
option_c: They replace security and medical professionals
option_d: They are paid the same as professional staff
explanation: Volunteers play a substantial part in running British sporting events, from local club fixtures to national occasions. At the London Olympic and Paralympic Games of 2012 some seventy thousand volunteers known as Games Makers welcomed spectators, directed crowds and assisted competitors, and they were widely credited with contributing to the atmosphere and success of the Games. Similar schemes have operated at the Commonwealth Games and other events. Volunteering of this kind is an example of the participation in community life that the official handbook encourages. Volunteers were awarded a commemorative medal and appeared in the closing ceremony. Many went on to volunteer at later events across the country. Their purple and red uniforms became a familiar sight that summer.

question: Which sport features the Challenge Cup as a major knockout competition?
option_a: Cricket
option_b: Rugby union
option_c: Hockey
option_d: Rugby league
explanation: The Challenge Cup is the leading knockout competition in rugby league, open to professional and amateur clubs, with the final traditionally played at Wembley Stadium and attracting large crowds from the northern heartlands of the sport. Rugby league split from rugby union in 1895 and is played with thirteen players a side, with its top competition being the Super League. Rugby union's knockout competitions include the Premiership play-offs and European club tournaments. The FA Cup is football's equivalent, and cricket has its own one-day knockout competitions between the counties. The competition dates from 1896 and has been played at Wembley since the 1920s. Women's and wheelchair versions of the competition are also contested.

question: What is Henley Royal Regatta?
option_a: A swimming competition held in the Lake District
option_b: A major rowing event held annually on the Thames in Oxfordshire
option_c: A sailing race around the Isle of Wight
option_d: A canoeing event held in Wales
explanation: Henley Royal Regatta is held each summer over several days on a stretch of the Thames at Henley-on-Thames in Oxfordshire and is among the best known rowing events in the world, attracting crews from many countries. Racing takes place between two boats at a time over a straight course, and the occasion is also a notable social event with its own dress codes in the stewards' enclosure. Cowes Week on the Isle of Wight is the leading British sailing regatta, and the Boat Race between Oxford and Cambridge is rowed in London each spring. The regatta has been held since 1839 and retains many of its Victorian customs. Spectators line the towpath along the length of the course.

question: Which of these is a traditional sport associated with Scottish Highland games?
option_a: Tossing the caber
option_b: Lawn tennis
option_c: Cricket
option_d: Cycling on a velodrome
explanation: Highland games are held across Scotland in the summer and feature traditional heavy athletic events including tossing the caber, a long wooden pole thrown end over end, putting the stone, and throwing the hammer and weights. The gatherings also include Highland dancing, piping competitions and tug of war, and they are accompanied by pipe bands. Many were revived or formalised in the nineteenth century, and the Braemar Gathering is traditionally attended by members of the royal family. The games are an important expression of Highland culture and attract visitors from around the world. Competitors traditionally wear kilts while taking part in the heavy events. Similar gatherings are held by Scottish communities living overseas.

question: Which sport in Britain uses the terms 'wicket', 'over' and 'innings'?
option_a: Rugby
option_b: Cricket
option_c: Hockey
option_d: Netball
explanation: These terms all belong to cricket, a sport with a long history in England and strong followings across the Commonwealth. A wicket refers both to the set of three stumps and two bails at each end of the pitch and to the dismissal of a batter, an over is a sequence of six deliveries bowled from one end, and an innings is the period during which a team bats. Cricket's vocabulary has entered everyday English in phrases such as a good innings and it's not cricket, meaning something is unfair. County cricket is played throughout the English summer. Village cricket on a summer green remains a familiar image of English rural life.

question: What does the term 'Team GB' refer to?
option_a: The Commonwealth Games team from Scotland
option_b: A Welsh rugby union side
option_c: The England football team
option_d: The combined British team at the Olympic Games
explanation: Team GB is the name used for the athletes representing Great Britain and Northern Ireland at the Olympic Games, where the four nations compete together rather than separately as they do in football, rugby union and the Commonwealth Games. The equivalent Paralympic team is known as ParalympicsGB. Team GB achieved its most successful modern Games at London in 2012 and has continued to perform strongly since, supported by lottery funding introduced in the 1990s that transformed the preparation available to elite British athletes across many sports. The team's kit is designed afresh for each Games and usually features the Union Flag. Athletes from all four nations, and from Crown dependencies, may be selected. The name has been used officially since the 1990s.

question: How is elite sport in the UK substantially funded?
option_a: Through National Lottery funding alongside commercial sponsorship
option_b: By compulsory contributions from clubs
option_c: Only from ticket sales
option_d: Entirely from income tax revenue
explanation: Since the National Lottery was established in the 1990s, a share of the money raised has been distributed to good causes including sport, and this funding has been used to support elite athletes with coaching, facilities and living costs so that they can train full time. British Olympic and Paralympic performance improved dramatically in the years that followed. Lottery money also supports grassroots facilities, the arts, heritage and community projects. Commercial sponsorship, broadcasting income and charitable fundraising provide further support, and local authorities fund leisure centres and playing fields. Funding is allocated to sports partly on the basis of their medal prospects, which has been debated. Athletes on the programme receive support grants towards living costs. The system is overseen by national sports agencies in each nation.

question: Which annual event sees thousands of runners raise money for charity in the capital?
option_a: The London Marathon
option_b: The Grand National
option_c: The Boat Race
option_d: Wimbledon
explanation: The London Marathon is held each spring and attracts tens of thousands of runners, from elite competitors to people in fancy dress raising money for charity, along the route between Greenwich and the Mall. It has raised enormous sums for charitable causes since it began in 1981 and is one of the largest fundraising events in the world. Similar mass participation events are held in Edinburgh, Manchester, Cardiff and Belfast, and the weekly parkrun, free and organised by volunteers, takes place in hundreds of parks across the United Kingdom on Saturday mornings. Places are allocated partly by ballot and partly through charity entries. Wheelchair races and elite events are held alongside the mass participation race.

question: Which of these best describes cricket's county championship?
option_a: A long-standing first-class competition between English and Welsh counties
option_b: An international tournament between Commonwealth countries
option_c: A one-day competition played only in Scotland
option_d: A schools competition organised by the government
explanation: The County Championship is the principal first-class domestic cricket competition in England and Wales, contested by eighteen county clubs over matches lasting four days and played through the summer. It has existed in an organised form since the late nineteenth century and is the traditional route through which players develop before selection for the national side. Counties also compete in one-day and Twenty20 competitions, which attract larger crowds. Scotland and Ireland have their own cricket structures and now compete as international sides in limited-overs competitions. The competition is divided into two divisions with promotion and relegation between them. Matches are often watched by small but devoted crowds. Several counties play some fixtures at outgrounds away from their main headquarters.

question: Which prize is awarded annually for the best novel written in English and published in the UK?
option_a: The BAFTA
option_b: The Booker Prize
option_c: The Mercury Prize
option_d: The Turner Prize
explanation: The Booker Prize, awarded each year for a full-length novel written in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland, is the country's most prominent literary award. Winning it transforms sales and reputations, and the announcement of the shortlist and the winner attracts wide coverage and argument. The prize was opened to writers of any nationality in 2014, having previously been restricted to those from the Commonwealth and Ireland, and there is a separate International Booker Prize for translated fiction, shared between author and translator. The Turner Prize is for contemporary art, the Mercury Prize for an album of the year, and BAFTAs are awarded for film and television. Together these awards form a familiar part of the British cultural calendar.

question: Which prize is awarded for contemporary visual art in Britain?
option_a: The Turner Prize
option_b: The Booker Prize
option_c: The Laurence Olivier Award
option_d: The Brit Award
explanation: The Turner Prize is awarded annually to a British visual artist and is named after the nineteenth-century painter J M W Turner. Established in 1984 and closely associated with Tate, it has become known for provoking public debate about what counts as art, with past winners including Damien Hirst, Rachel Whiteread, Grayson Perry and Antony Gormley. The shortlisted works are exhibited before the winner is announced, and the exhibition travels to a different city in some years. Brit Awards are given for popular music, the Laurence Olivier Awards for London theatre, and the Booker Prize for fiction. The prize regularly attracts as much criticism as praise, which its supporters regard as part of its purpose.

question: Who was the composer of The Planets?
option_a: Benjamin Britten
option_b: Henry Purcell
option_c: Edward Elgar
option_d: Gustav Holst
explanation: Gustav Holst, an English composer of Swedish descent, wrote the orchestral suite The Planets in the years around the First World War, giving each movement the character of a planet as understood in astrology. Its opening movement, Mars, and the broad melody in Jupiter, later set to the hymn 'I Vow to Thee, My Country', are among the best known passages in British music. Edward Elgar composed the Enigma Variations and the Pomp and Circumstance marches, one of which supplies the tune of 'Land of Hope and Glory'. Benjamin Britten wrote operas including Peter Grimes and the War Requiem, and Henry Purcell was the leading English composer of the seventeenth century.

question: Which composer wrote the Enigma Variations and the Pomp and Circumstance marches?
option_a: Gustav Holst
option_b: Edward Elgar
option_c: William Walton
option_d: Ralph Vaughan Williams
explanation: Sir Edward Elgar was the leading English composer of his generation and wrote the Enigma Variations, in which each movement portrays a friend, as well as the Pomp and Circumstance marches, the first of which provides the melody of 'Land of Hope and Glory' sung at the Last Night of the Proms. He also composed the oratorio The Dream of Gerontius and a cello concerto written after the First World War. Ralph Vaughan Williams drew on English folk song in works such as The Lark Ascending, and Sir William Walton composed film scores and ceremonial music. Their work forms the core of what is often called the English musical renaissance.

question: Which British composer wrote the opera Peter Grimes?
option_a: Edward Elgar
option_b: Andrew Lloyd Webber
option_c: Henry Purcell
option_d: Benjamin Britten
explanation: Benjamin Britten composed Peter Grimes, first performed in 1945 and set in a fishing community on the Suffolk coast, and it is generally regarded as the most important English opera of the twentieth century. He wrote many other works including the War Requiem, composed for the consecration of the rebuilt Coventry Cathedral, and The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra. He founded the Aldeburgh Festival in Suffolk, which continues today. Henry Purcell wrote Dido and Aeneas in the seventeenth century, Elgar belongs to the late Victorian and Edwardian period, and Andrew Lloyd Webber is a composer of musical theatre rather than opera.

question: Who is generally considered the greatest English composer of the seventeenth century?
option_a: Thomas Tallis
option_b: Henry Purcell
option_c: Benjamin Britten
option_d: George Frideric Handel
explanation: Henry Purcell, organist of Westminster Abbey and composer to the royal court, wrote church music, odes, songs and theatre music, together with the opera Dido and Aeneas, and he is regarded as the outstanding English composer of his era. He died young in 1695 and is buried in Westminster Abbey. George Frideric Handel was born in Germany, settled in London and became a British subject, composing Messiah, Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks; Zadok the Priest, written for a coronation, has been sung at every British coronation since. Thomas Tallis and William Byrd were Tudor composers of church music of great distinction.

question: Which German-born composer settled in Britain and wrote Messiah and Water Music?
option_a: Felix Mendelssohn
option_b: Johann Sebastian Bach
option_c: Joseph Haydn
option_d: George Frideric Handel
explanation: George Frideric Handel was born in Germany, worked in Italy and settled in London, where he became a British subject and spent the rest of his life. He composed Italian operas, then the English oratorios for which he is now best known, including Messiah with its Hallelujah chorus, as well as the orchestral Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks. His anthem Zadok the Priest has been performed at every British coronation since 1727. He is buried in Westminster Abbey. Haydn and Mendelssohn both visited Britain and wrote works for British audiences, but neither settled permanently in the country as Handel did.

question: What are the Brit Awards?
option_a: Prizes awarded for new British films only
option_b: Awards given for scientific research
option_c: Honours conferred by the monarch
option_d: Annual awards for popular music in Britain
explanation: The Brit Awards are the British recording industry's annual awards for popular music, presented at a televised ceremony with categories for British and international artists, albums, songs and newcomers. They have been held since 1977 and are often remembered for the live performances and occasional controversies that accompany them. The Mercury Prize is a separate award for the best album of the year by a British or Irish act, judged by a panel rather than by sales. British popular music has been internationally successful for decades, from the Beatles and the Rolling Stones through punk, new wave, Britpop, dance music and grime.

question: Which British music festival is held each summer at Worthy Farm in Somerset?
option_a: The Proms
option_b: The Edinburgh Festival
option_c: Notting Hill Carnival
option_d: Glastonbury
explanation: The Glastonbury Festival of Contemporary Performing Arts is held over several days in June on a farm in Somerset and is among the largest greenfield music and performing arts festivals in the world, attracting well over a hundred thousand people who camp on the site. It features many stages of music alongside theatre, circus, comedy and dance, and it donates substantial sums to charity. Tickets usually sell out within minutes of going on sale. Other large British festivals include Reading and Leeds, the Isle of Wight Festival, Download and TRNSMT in Glasgow, and there are many smaller events throughout the summer.

question: Which instrument is particularly associated with Scottish traditional music?
option_a: The bagpipes
option_b: The accordion only
option_c: The fiddle only
option_d: The harp
explanation: The Great Highland bagpipe is strongly associated with Scotland, played solo and in pipe bands at Highland games, ceremonies, weddings and funerals, and by military regiments. Competitions in piping form part of Highland gatherings. The fiddle and accordion are also central to Scottish traditional and dance music, particularly at ceilidhs. The harp, or telyn, is the national instrument of Wales, where choral singing, especially by male voice choirs, has a particularly strong tradition, and the Welsh have a long history of song competitions at eisteddfodau. Ireland and Northern Ireland have their own rich traditions of fiddle, flute and bodhran playing.

question: What is a ceilidh?
option_a: A social gathering with traditional music and dancing
option_b: A type of Highland athletic competition
option_c: A formal state banquet
option_d: A church service held in Gaelic
explanation: A ceilidh, pronounced kay-lee, is an informal social event with traditional music and dancing, common in Scotland and Ireland and held at weddings, new year celebrations and community gatherings throughout the United Kingdom. A caller usually explains the steps so that people who have never danced them before can take part, and the dances are performed in sets, lines or circles to fiddle, accordion and drum. The word comes from Gaelic and originally meant a visit or gathering for storytelling and song. Similar events in England are often called barn dances, and Welsh folk dancing has its own distinct traditions.

question: What is pantomime?
option_a: A comic musical stage show performed around Christmas, usually based on a fairy tale
option_b: An opera sung in Italian
option_c: A religious play performed at Easter
option_d: A silent performance using only gesture
explanation: Pantomime is a distinctively British form of theatre staged around Christmas and the new year, based loosely on fairy tales such as Cinderella, Aladdin or Jack and the Beanstalk. It mixes slapstick comedy, songs, topical jokes and audience participation, with the audience expected to boo the villain and shout warnings such as 'he's behind you'. Conventions include a dame played by a male actor and a principal boy traditionally played by a woman. Pantomimes are staged in theatres across the country and are for many children the first live theatre they see, which makes them commercially important to regional venues.

question: What is the West End known for?
option_a: A region of Scotland famous for whisky
option_b: London's main commercial theatre district
option_c: The financial district of the capital
option_d: A national park in northern England
explanation: The West End of London is the city's principal theatre district, with dozens of venues staging plays, musicals and comedy, and it is often compared with Broadway in New York. Long-running musicals such as Les Misérables and The Phantom of the Opera have played for decades, and new plays and revivals appear alongside them. The National Theatre and Shakespeare's Globe lie on the South Bank of the Thames, and the Royal Shakespeare Company is based at Stratford-upon-Avon. Theatre also thrives outside London, in repertory theatres and in the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the largest arts festival in the world. Ticket prices vary widely, and discounted same-day seats are sold from a booth in Leicester Square.

question: Which composer is known for musicals including The Phantom of the Opera and Cats?
option_a: Gustav Holst
option_b: Edward Elgar
option_c: Andrew Lloyd Webber
option_d: Benjamin Britten
explanation: Lord Lloyd-Webber has written many of the most commercially successful musicals in the world, including Jesus Christ Superstar, Evita, Cats and The Phantom of the Opera, several with the lyricist Tim Rice. His shows have run for decades in the West End and on Broadway and have been seen by enormous audiences internationally. He also owns several London theatres. British musical theatre has a long history, running back through Gilbert and Sullivan's Victorian comic operas, and the West End remains one of the two great centres of the form alongside New York, employing very large numbers of performers and technical staff.

question: Which award is given for achievement in British theatre?
option_a: The Laurence Olivier Awards
option_b: The Booker Prize
option_c: The Turner Prize
option_d: The Mercury Prize
explanation: The Laurence Olivier Awards, named after the actor and director Lord Olivier, are the leading British awards for professional theatre in London, covering plays, musicals, opera and dance, and they are broadly equivalent to the Tony Awards in New York. Olivier himself was among the most celebrated actors of the twentieth century and was the first director of the National Theatre. Other major British awards include the BAFTAs for film and television, the Brit Awards and Mercury Prize for music, the Turner Prize for visual art and the Booker Prize for fiction, each with its own ceremony and following. The awards ceremony is held in the spring and is broadcast to a national audience.

question: Which award is presented by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts?
option_a: The Palme d'Or
option_b: The Oscar
option_c: The Golden Globe
option_d: The BAFTA
explanation: BAFTA awards are presented by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts for achievement in film, television, games and children's media, and the film ceremony is held each year shortly before the Academy Awards in the United States. The trophy is a bronze mask. British film has a long and distinguished history, from Alfred Hitchcock and David Lean to the Ealing comedies, the James Bond series, the films of Ken Loach and Mike Leigh and the animation of Nick Park's Wallace and Gromit. Studios at Pinewood, Shepperton and Leavesden produce many international productions. The academy also runs education and outreach schemes for people entering the industry.

question: Which British film director became famous for suspense films such as Psycho and The Birds?
option_a: Ken Loach
option_b: Alfred Hitchcock
option_c: Danny Boyle
option_d: David Lean
explanation: Sir Alfred Hitchcock began his career in British silent cinema and went on to become one of the most influential directors in film history, known as the master of suspense for works including The 39 Steps, Rear Window, Vertigo, Psycho and The Birds. He moved to Hollywood but retained his British identity and humour. Sir David Lean directed Brief Encounter, The Bridge on the River Kwai and Lawrence of Arabia, Ken Loach is known for films examining social conditions in Britain, and Danny Boyle directed Trainspotting and Slumdog Millionaire and staged the London Olympic opening ceremony in 2012. He famously appeared in brief cameo roles in almost all of his own films.

question: Which British animator created Wallace and Gromit?
option_a: Richard Curtis
option_b: Steve Coogan
option_c: Nick Hornby
option_d: Nick Park
explanation: Nick Park created the characters Wallace and Gromit at Aardman Animations in Bristol, using painstaking stop-motion modelling in which figures are moved fractionally between frames. The films have won several Academy Awards, and the studio also produced Chicken Run and Shaun the Sheep. British animation and visual effects work has an international reputation, and studios in London and Bristol contribute to many major productions. Richard Curtis wrote screenplays including Four Weddings and a Funeral and Notting Hill, Nick Hornby is a novelist and screenwriter, and Steve Coogan is a comic actor and writer. A single day's filming may produce only a few seconds of finished footage.

question: Which fictional British secret agent has appeared in a long-running film series?
option_a: Sherlock Holmes
option_b: James Bond
option_c: Doctor Who
option_d: Harry Potter
explanation: James Bond, the secret agent created by the novelist Ian Fleming, has appeared in one of the longest-running film series in cinema history, beginning with Dr No in 1962 and with the role played by several different actors including Sean Connery, Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. The films are largely made in Britain and have become part of the country's cultural export. Sherlock Holmes, created by Arthur Conan Doyle, has also been adapted repeatedly, Harry Potter is the schoolboy wizard of J K Rowling's novels, and Doctor Who is a long-running BBC science fiction television series first broadcast in 1963.

question: Who wrote the Harry Potter novels?
option_a: Philip Pullman
option_b: J K Rowling
option_c: C S Lewis
option_d: Roald Dahl
explanation: J K Rowling wrote the seven Harry Potter novels, published between 1997 and 2007, which became among the best-selling books in history and were adapted into a hugely successful film series made largely in Britain. She wrote much of the first book in Edinburgh, where she still lives. Philip Pullman wrote the His Dark Materials trilogy, Roald Dahl wrote children's books including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and Matilda, and C S Lewis wrote the Chronicles of Narnia. British children's literature has an exceptionally strong tradition, running back through Beatrix Potter, A A Milne, Kenneth Grahame and Lewis Carroll. The books have been translated into dozens of languages and sold hundreds of millions of copies.

question: Who wrote The Lord of the Rings?
option_a: C S Lewis
option_b: George Orwell
option_c: J R R Tolkien
option_d: Evelyn Waugh
explanation: J R R Tolkien, a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, creating an elaborate imagined world with its own languages, histories and mythologies that has influenced fantasy writing ever since. The books have been translated into many languages and adapted into successful films. C S Lewis, his friend and fellow Oxford scholar, wrote the Chronicles of Narnia. George Orwell wrote Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, works of political warning whose vocabulary has entered everyday English, and Evelyn Waugh wrote satirical novels including Decline and Fall and Brideshead Revisited. He served in the First World War, an experience often said to colour the books' battle scenes.

question: Who wrote the novel Nineteen Eighty-Four?
option_a: George Orwell
option_b: Aldous Huxley
option_c: H G Wells
option_d: Graham Greene
explanation: George Orwell, the pen name of Eric Blair, wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949, a novel depicting a totalitarian state that watches and controls its citizens, and Animal Farm, an allegory of revolution betrayed. Terms from the book, including Big Brother, thoughtcrime and newspeak, have entered everyday English, and the adjective Orwellian is widely used. He also wrote reportage on poverty and on the Spanish Civil War. Aldous Huxley wrote Brave New World, H G Wells wrote early science fiction including The War of the Worlds, and Graham Greene wrote novels including Brighton Rock. He drew on his experience of wartime propaganda work while writing the novel.

question: Who is the best-selling British crime novelist, creator of Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple?
option_a: P D James
option_b: Dorothy L Sayers
option_c: Agatha Christie
option_d: Ruth Rendell
explanation: Agatha Christie wrote more than sixty detective novels and numerous short stories and is among the best-selling novelists of all time, creating the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot and the village sleuth Miss Marple. Her play The Mousetrap ran continuously in the West End for decades, the longest-running production in theatrical history. Dorothy L Sayers created Lord Peter Wimsey in the same period, and P D James and Ruth Rendell were leading British crime writers of the later twentieth century. Crime fiction remains one of the most popular genres with British readers and a staple of British television drama. Her disappearance for eleven days in 1926 remains an unexplained episode in her own life.

question: What is the role of the Poet Laureate?
option_a: An official who awards literary prizes
option_b: An honorary post held by a poet, who may write verse for national occasions
option_c: A civil servant who censors published poetry
option_d: The head of the English department at Oxford
explanation: The Poet Laureate is an honorary position within the royal household, held by a poet appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister, who may compose verse to mark significant national events, although there is no longer any obligation to do so. The post dates from the seventeenth century and was once held for life; it is now held for a fixed term of ten years. Past holders include William Wordsworth, Alfred Lord Tennyson, John Betjeman and Ted Hughes, and Carol Ann Duffy became the first woman appointed. The role carries a small stipend and, traditionally, a butt of sherry.

question: What is Poets' Corner?
option_a: A literary festival held in Hay-on-Wye
option_b: A weekly poetry programme on BBC radio
option_c: A section of the British Library holding poetry manuscripts
option_d: An area of Westminster Abbey where many writers are buried or commemorated
explanation: Poets' Corner is part of the south transept of Westminster Abbey where many of Britain's greatest writers are buried or commemorated with memorials. Geoffrey Chaucer was the first to be buried there, and the tradition grew up around his tomb. Those commemorated include Shakespeare, Dickens, Hardy, Tennyson, the Brontë sisters, Jane Austen, T S Eliot and Dylan Thomas, among many others. Westminster Abbey itself has been the setting for coronations since 1066 and for many royal weddings and funerals, and it also contains the graves of scientists including Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin. Memorials continue to be added, and the honour is regarded as one of the highest in British letters.

question: Which Welsh poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
option_a: Gerard Manley Hopkins
option_b: Wilfred Owen
option_c: R S Thomas
option_d: Dylan Thomas
explanation: Dylan Thomas, born in Swansea, wrote the villanelle beginning 'Do not go gentle into that good night', addressed to his dying father, and the radio play Under Milk Wood, which portrays a day in the life of a small Welsh seaside town. His readings and broadcasts made him famous, and he died in New York in 1953 at the age of thirty-nine. R S Thomas was another major Welsh poet of the twentieth century, Wilfred Owen wrote the best-known English poetry of the First World War, and Gerard Manley Hopkins was a Victorian poet whose work was published only after his death.

question: Which poet is best known for writing about the experience of the First World War?
option_a: William Wordsworth
option_b: Robert Browning
option_c: John Keats
option_d: Wilfred Owen
explanation: Wilfred Owen wrote the most widely read English poetry of the First World War, including 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', describing the suffering of soldiers in terms that directly challenged patriotic rhetoric at home. He was killed in action a week before the armistice in 1918, and most of his work was published after his death, partly through the efforts of his friend Siegfried Sassoon, another notable war poet. Benjamin Britten set several of his poems in the War Requiem. Wordsworth, Keats and Browning belong to the Romantic and Victorian periods of the previous century. His mother received the telegram announcing his death as the armistice bells were ringing.

question: Which British painter is known for industrial scenes with 'matchstick' figures?
option_a: Francis Bacon
option_b: David Hockney
option_c: John Constable
option_d: L S Lowry
explanation: L S Lowry painted the industrial towns of north-west England, with mills, chimneys and crowds of thin, stylised figures that became known as matchstick men, working for most of his life as a rent collector in Salford and painting in the evenings. A gallery named after him stands at Salford Quays. David Hockney is among the most celebrated living British artists, known for Californian swimming pool paintings and Yorkshire landscapes, Francis Bacon painted disturbing figurative work in the mid twentieth century, and John Constable was the great painter of the English countryside in the early nineteenth century. He repeatedly declined public honours, including a knighthood, during his lifetime.

question: Which British sculptors are known for large abstract and figurative works of the twentieth century?
option_a: Gilbert and Sullivan
option_b: Reynolds and Gainsborough
option_c: Turner and Constable
option_d: Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth
explanation: Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth were the leading British sculptors of the twentieth century. Moore is known for large reclining figures and family groups in bronze and stone, often placed in open landscapes, and Hepworth for abstract forms pierced with holes and strung with wire, many produced at her studio in St Ives in Cornwall, now a museum. Both achieved international reputations, and their work stands in public spaces around the world. Antony Gormley's Angel of the North near Gateshead and his figures on Crosby beach continue the tradition of large-scale British public sculpture. Hepworth died in a fire at her St Ives studio in 1975, and the site is preserved as a museum.

question: What is the Angel of the North?
option_a: A bridge across the Tyne
option_b: A monument to Admiral Nelson
option_c: A large steel sculpture by Antony Gormley near Gateshead
option_d: A cathedral in York
explanation: The Angel of the North is a steel sculpture by Sir Antony Gormley standing beside the A1 road near Gateshead in north-east England. Completed in 1998, it is around twenty metres tall with a wingspan wider than its height, designed to withstand high winds, and it has become a landmark instantly associated with the region. It was controversial when proposed and is now widely admired. Gormley's other public works include Another Place, a hundred cast-iron figures standing on the beach at Crosby near Liverpool, and the Fourth Plinth project in Trafalgar Square has hosted a rotating series of contemporary commissions.

question: Which gallery in London houses the national collection of Western European paintings?
option_a: The Science Museum
option_b: The Natural History Museum
option_c: The National Gallery
option_d: The British Museum
explanation: The National Gallery in Trafalgar Square holds the national collection of Western European paintings from the thirteenth to the early twentieth century, including works by Leonardo, Titian, Rembrandt, Van Gogh, Turner and Constable, and admission to the permanent collection is free. Tate Britain holds British art from the sixteenth century onwards and Tate Modern international modern and contemporary art. The British Museum houses antiquities and objects from cultures across the world, the Science Museum and the Natural History Museum are in South Kensington, and the National Portrait Gallery holds portraits of notable British figures. The gallery was founded in 1824 when Parliament bought a private collection for the nation.

question: What is notable about admission to many national museums in the UK?
option_a: A licence must be bought in advance
option_b: Entry to the permanent collections is free
option_c: Only school groups may visit
option_d: Entry is restricted to British citizens
explanation: Admission to the permanent collections of the national museums and galleries in the United Kingdom is free, a policy intended to make the collections accessible to everyone, though charges are usually made for special exhibitions and donations are invited. Free entry applies at the British Museum, the National Gallery, Tate Britain and Tate Modern, the Natural History and Science Museums, the National Museum of Scotland, National Museum Wales and others. Many local authority museums are also free. Historic houses and castles, by contrast, usually charge, and bodies such as the National Trust and English Heritage rely on membership and admission income.

question: Which architect designed St Paul's Cathedral and many City churches after the Great Fire?
option_a: Robert Adam
option_b: Sir Edwin Lutyens
option_c: Sir Christopher Wren
option_d: Sir Norman Foster
explanation: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral and more than fifty parish churches in the City of London after the Great Fire of 1666, as well as the Royal Naval Hospital at Greenwich and buildings in Oxford and Cambridge. His great dome remains one of London's defining sights. Robert Adam was the leading designer of Georgian interiors and country houses, Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph and much of New Delhi, and Lord Foster is among the most prominent contemporary British architects, responsible for the Gherkin in London, the Millennium Bridge and the remodelled Reichstag in Berlin. His epitaph inside the cathedral invites the reader to look around for his monument.

question: Who designed the Houses of Parliament in their present form?
option_a: Sir Christopher Wren
option_b: Sir Norman Foster
option_c: Inigo Jones
option_d: Sir Charles Barry with Augustus Pugin
explanation: The Palace of Westminster was largely destroyed by fire in 1834 and was rebuilt to designs by Sir Charles Barry, with Augustus Pugin responsible for the elaborate Gothic detail, interiors, furnishings and the clock tower that houses the bell known as Big Ben. The choice of a Gothic style was deliberate, intended to evoke medieval English tradition rather than classical Europe. Westminster Hall, dating from the eleventh century with a magnificent hammerbeam roof, survived the fire and remains part of the building. The palace is a World Heritage Site and is undergoing a long programme of restoration. Pugin died young, exhausted by the enormous volume of detailed design work involved.

question: What is Big Ben?
option_a: A statue outside Buckingham Palace
option_b: The dome of St Paul's Cathedral
option_c: The clock face itself
option_d: The great bell in the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament
explanation: Big Ben is strictly the name of the great bell housed in the clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, although the name is commonly applied to the tower and clock as well. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee. The bell's chimes are broadcast on radio and mark the hour for significant national occasions, including new year. The clock was famed for its accuracy when built in the nineteenth century. The tower underwent extensive restoration in recent years, during which the bell was largely silent. The bell weighs more than thirteen tonnes and cracked shortly after it was first installed.

question: Which style of architecture is associated with Georgian Britain?
option_a: Classical proportions with symmetrical facades and sash windows
option_b: Timber framing with exposed beams
option_c: Steel frames and glass curtain walls
option_d: Pointed arches and flying buttresses
explanation: Georgian architecture, dating from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, drew on classical Greek and Roman models, favouring symmetry, careful proportion, restrained decoration, and terraces of brick or stone houses with sash windows and fanlights above the doors. Bath, Edinburgh's New Town, Cheltenham and parts of London and Dublin are rich in examples. Pointed arches and buttresses belong to the medieval Gothic style seen in cathedrals such as Salisbury and York, which was revived in the Victorian period for churches, town halls and the Houses of Parliament. Steel and glass belong to modern architecture of the twentieth century onwards. Many Georgian terraces were built speculatively and are now highly sought after as housing.

question: Which cathedral has the tallest spire in Britain?
option_a: York Minster
option_b: Durham
option_c: Salisbury
option_d: Canterbury
explanation: Salisbury Cathedral in Wiltshire has the tallest church spire in Britain, rising to around a hundred and twenty-three metres, and the cathedral is remarkable for having been built largely in a single architectural style over a short period in the thirteenth century. It also holds one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta. York Minster is the largest medieval cathedral in northern Europe and is celebrated for its stained glass, Canterbury is the mother church of the Anglican Communion and the site of Thomas Becket's murder, and Durham Cathedral is a masterpiece of Norman architecture standing above the River Wear.

question: What is the Eden Project?
option_a: A nature reserve in the Scottish Highlands
option_b: A botanical library in Kew
option_c: A garden created for the Great Exhibition
option_d: A complex of giant biomes housing plants from different climates, in Cornwall
explanation: The Eden Project, built in a disused china clay pit near St Austell in Cornwall and opened in 2001, consists of enormous linked domes, known as biomes, made of hexagonal transparent panels, which house plants from tropical rainforest and Mediterranean climates alongside extensive outdoor gardens. It combines a visitor attraction with education about plants, conservation and sustainability and has become a major driver of tourism in the county. The Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew in west London, a World Heritage Site, hold one of the world's most important plant collections and seed banks. The biomes are the largest greenhouses in the world and use lightweight plastic panels rather than glass.

question: What is the London Eye?
option_a: A cable car across the river at Greenwich
option_b: A large observation wheel on the South Bank of the Thames
option_c: A viewing platform on top of the Shard
option_d: A telescope at the Royal Observatory
explanation: The London Eye is a giant observation wheel on the South Bank of the Thames, opposite the Houses of Parliament, which opened to mark the millennium and has become one of the capital's most recognisable landmarks. Its enclosed capsules carry passengers slowly round, giving wide views across the city. Other well known viewpoints include the Shard, the tallest building in the country, and the Monument commemorating the Great Fire. The Royal Observatory at Greenwich, where the prime meridian of zero longitude is marked, is another major attraction and gives its name to Greenwich Mean Time. A single revolution takes about half an hour, and the wheel turns slowly enough for passengers to board while moving.

question: What is significant about Greenwich in London?
option_a: It is the site of the Houses of Parliament
option_b: It is where the Great Fire of London began
option_c: It is the oldest university city in England
option_d: It gives its name to Greenwich Mean Time and marks the prime meridian
explanation: Greenwich, in south-east London, is the site of the Royal Observatory, founded in 1675 to improve navigation at sea, and the prime meridian of zero degrees longitude runs through it, so that longitude everywhere on earth is measured from that line. Greenwich Mean Time became the basis of world timekeeping. The area is a World Heritage Site and also contains the National Maritime Museum, the Old Royal Naval College designed by Wren, and the preserved tea clipper Cutty Sark. British Summer Time, an hour ahead, operates from late March to late October each year. Visitors can stand with one foot in each hemisphere on the marked meridian line.

question: Which of these is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the UK?
option_a: There are no World Heritage Sites in the UK
option_b: Only Buckingham Palace
option_c: Only sites in England qualify
option_d: Stonehenge, Edinburgh's Old and New Towns, the Giant's Causeway and many others
explanation: The United Kingdom has more than thirty World Heritage Sites recognised by UNESCO for their cultural or natural significance. They include Stonehenge and Avebury, the Tower of London, Westminster Abbey and the Palace of Westminster, the city of Bath, Hadrian's Wall, Edinburgh's Old and New Towns, the Forth Bridge, the castles of Edward I in Gwynedd, Blaenavon industrial landscape in Wales, the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland, Ironbridge Gorge and the Lake District. The designation brings international recognition and a duty to protect the site for future generations, and many are major visitor attractions. Sites can be removed from the list if development threatens the qualities that led to their listing.

question: What is the National Trust?
option_a: A bank owned by the state
option_b: A government department managing public land
option_c: An organisation that runs the national museums
option_d: A charity that preserves historic buildings, gardens and countryside for the public
explanation: The National Trust is a charity, founded in 1895 and independent of government, which cares for historic houses, castles, gardens, industrial monuments, farmland, woods, villages and long stretches of coastline in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, with a separate National Trust for Scotland performing the same role there. It is one of the largest membership organisations in the country, and members visit its properties free of charge. Its work depends heavily on volunteers. English Heritage and its equivalents in the other nations look after many ancient monuments and ruins, including Stonehenge and numerous castles. It owns hundreds of miles of coastline, much of it acquired through a long-running appeal.

question: How many national parks are there in the UK, broadly speaking?
option_a: Fifteen, spread across England, Wales and Scotland
option_b: Forty, one in each county
option_c: Two, both in Scotland
option_d: None; the UK has no national parks
explanation: There are fifteen national parks in the United Kingdom, ten in England, three in Wales and two in Scotland, including the Lake District, Snowdonia, the Peak District, the Cairngorms and the Brecon Beacons, the last two now officially named Eryri and Bannau Brycheiniog. Northern Ireland has no national parks but does have designated areas of outstanding natural beauty.
