As a woman from a poor background she was excluded from the scientific societies of the day and rarely received public credit at the time, though her expertise was privately acknowledged by leading geologists who bought and studied her specimens. A museum in Lyme Regis and a recent film have brought her story to a much wider audience.

question: What is the Jurassic Coast?
option_a: A stretch of the Northumberland coast with Roman remains
option_b: An area of the Scottish coast noted for seabirds
option_c: A World Heritage Site along the Dorset and east Devon coast, famous for fossils
option_d: A section of the Welsh coast path
explanation: The Jurassic Coast runs along the shoreline of Dorset and east Devon and was designated a World Heritage Site for the exceptional record of earth history exposed in its cliffs, spanning many millions of years. It is renowned for fossils, which continue to be revealed by erosion, and for landmarks including Durdle Door and Lulworth Cove. Mary Anning made her celebrated discoveries there in the nineteenth century. The South West Coast Path, the longest national trail in England, follows the coast, and the area attracts geologists, walkers and holidaymakers in large numbers each year. Visitors are warned that the cliffs are unstable and that rockfalls occur without warning.

question: What is the honours system in the UK?
option_a: A system of ranking schools by examination results
option_b: Awards such as knighthoods and MBEs given for achievement and public service
option_c: A scheme awarding grants to charities
option_d: The order of precedence in the House of Lords
explanation: The honours system recognises achievement and service through awards announced twice a year, at new year and on the monarch's official birthday, and conferred at investitures usually held at Buckingham Palace or Windsor Castle. The Order of the British Empire, with grades including MBE, OBE and CBE, is the most commonly awarded, and knighthoods and damehoods carry the titles Sir and Dame. Nominations can be made by any member of the public as well as by government departments. Recipients include people from every walk of life, and a proportion of awards goes to volunteers and community workers rather than to public figures.

question: What does the Duke of Edinburgh's Award scheme offer young people?
option_a: Membership of the armed forces reserve
option_b: A scholarship for university study
option_c: A programme of volunteering, skills, physical activity and expeditions
option_d: A guaranteed apprenticeship
explanation: The Duke of Edinburgh's Award, founded in 1956 by Prince Philip, challenges young people to complete sections covering volunteering, developing a skill, physical recreation and an expedition, with a residential element at the highest level. Awards are made at bronze, silver and gold, the last presented at a ceremony attended by a member of the royal family. The scheme operates through schools, youth groups and other organisations and has spread to many countries. Other large youth organisations in Britain include the Scouts, the Guides, the Boys' and Girls' Brigades and the cadet forces, all relying heavily on volunteer leaders. Employers and universities often regard completion of the gold award as evidence of commitment.

question: Which youth movement was founded in Britain by Robert Baden-Powell?
option_a: The National Trust
option_b: The Duke of Edinburgh's Award
option_c: The Scouts
option_d: The Salvation Army
explanation: The Scout movement was founded by Robert Baden-Powell, a former army officer, following an experimental camp on Brownsea Island in Dorset in 1907 and the publication of his book Scouting for Boys. It emphasised outdoor activity, practical skills, self-reliance and service to others, and it spread rapidly around the world, with the Girl Guides founded shortly afterwards. Both organisations now admit young people of any sex in the United Kingdom and continue to operate through local groups run largely by volunteers. Camping, hiking, badges for skills learned and a promise made on joining remain central features. Millions of young people worldwide now belong to Scouting or Guiding organisations.

question: Which organisation provides lifeboat rescue around the coasts of the UK and Ireland?
option_a: The National Trust
option_b: The Royal Navy
option_c: The RNLI
option_d: The Coastguard alone
explanation: The Royal National Lifeboat Institution is a charity, funded by donations rather than by the government, which operates lifeboats from stations around the coasts of the United Kingdom and Ireland and provides lifeguards on many beaches. Its crews are overwhelmingly volunteers who leave work or home at short notice when called out, and the service has saved many thousands of lives since its foundation in 1824. His Majesty's Coastguard, a government service, coordinates maritime search and rescue and calls on the RNLI, helicopters and other resources. Mountain rescue teams operate on a similar voluntary basis in upland areas. Its crews launch thousands of times a year, in all weathers and at any hour. Lifeboat stations hold open days and fundraising events throughout the summer.

question: Which British institution collects and preserves published works?
option_a: The Royal Society
option_b: The British Library
option_c: The British Museum
option_d: The National Archives
explanation: The British Library in London is the national library of the United Kingdom and one of the largest libraries in the world, entitled under legal deposit to receive a copy of every book published in the country. Its collections include manuscripts such as Magna Carta and the Lindisfarne Gospels, historic newspapers, maps, sound recordings and the papers of many writers. Readers may apply for a pass to consult material in its reading rooms. The National Archives at Kew hold the records of government, the British Museum holds antiquities and objects from around the world, and the National Library of Scotland and National Library of Wales perform comparable roles.

question: How do people in Britain most commonly follow the news today?
option_a: Through notices posted in town halls
option_b: Exclusively through government bulletins
option_c: Only through printed newspapers
option_d: Through a mixture of television, radio, newspapers and online sources
explanation: News reaches people in Britain through a wide range of sources. Television bulletins and rolling news channels, radio programmes such as those on BBC Radio 4 and commercial stations, national and local newspapers and their websites, and social media and news applications all play a part, with online consumption having grown rapidly and print circulation falling. Broadcasters are required by law to be impartial in their news coverage, while newspapers may and do take clear political positions. There is no state control of editorial content, and the ability of journalists to scrutinise those in power is regarded as an important safeguard.

question: Which body regulates broadcasting and telecommunications in the UK?
option_a: The Press Association
option_b: The BBC Trust
option_c: Ofcom
option_d: The Home Office
explanation: Ofcom is the independent regulator for broadcasting, telecommunications and postal services in the United Kingdom. It issues licences to television and radio broadcasters, enforces standards on matters such as impartiality in news, harm, offence and the protection of children, investigates complaints about programmes, and oversees competition and consumer protection in telephone and broadband markets. It also has responsibilities in relation to online safety. The press is not regulated by Ofcom but by self-regulatory bodies that handle complaints about accuracy and conduct, an arrangement that has been the subject of considerable public debate and a major public inquiry. It can impose fines on broadcasters and, in serious cases, revoke a licence altogether.

question: What is the Post Office's role in British communities?
option_a: Issuing passports and driving licences directly
option_b: Providing postal, banking and government services, often within another shop
option_c: Printing all national newspapers
option_d: Collecting council tax
explanation: Post offices provide postal services, sell stamps and handle parcels, and they also offer banking facilities, foreign currency, vehicle tax, passport checking services and access to some government schemes, which makes them particularly important in rural areas and small towns. Many branches are now operated within newsagents, convenience stores or village shops rather than as separate premises. Royal Mail, which delivers letters and parcels, was separated from the Post Office and sold to private investors in 2013. A long-running scandal involving faulty accounting software led to the wrongful prosecution of many subpostmasters and to a public inquiry. Campaigns to keep village post offices open are common when closures are proposed.

question: What is meant by the term 'the Union' in a British context?
option_a: A single trade union covering all workers
option_b: An association of British universities
option_c: The United Kingdom's former membership of the European Union
option_d: The political union of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
explanation: The Union refers to the constitutional union of the four nations that make up the United Kingdom, brought together over several centuries: Wales joined with England under Tudor legislation, the crowns of England and Scotland were united in 1603 and their parliaments in 1707, and Ireland was joined in 1801, with most of it leaving in 1922. Debate about the future of the Union remains live, particularly in Scotland, where a referendum on independence was held in 2014, and in Northern Ireland, where the Belfast Agreement provides for a border poll in certain circumstances. Supporters of the Union are described as unionists, and those seeking separation as nationalists. Opinion on the question differs considerably between the four nations.

question: What is a 'bank holiday Monday' typically in the British calendar?
option_a: The first Monday of every month
option_b: A day on which taxes are due
option_c: A day when only banks are closed
option_d: A Monday designated as a public holiday, giving a long weekend
explanation: Several British public holidays fall on a Monday, including Easter Monday, the early May bank holiday, the spring bank holiday at the end of May and the late summer bank holiday in August, so that they create three-day weekends. When Christmas Day, Boxing Day or New Year's Day falls on a Saturday or Sunday, a substitute holiday is given on the following weekday. Scotland has a slightly different set of holidays, including 2 January and St Andrew's Day, and Northern Ireland adds St Patrick's Day and the twelfth of July to the calendar. Roads and tourist attractions are typically at their busiest on these long weekends. Some employers require staff to work them, with time off given in lieu.

question: Which of these is a well-known long-distance walking route in Britain?
option_a: The Pennine Way
option_b: The A1 trunk road
option_c: The Caledonian Canal
option_d: The Grand Union Canal
explanation: The Pennine Way, opened in 1965, was the first national trail in Britain and runs for more than four hundred kilometres along the hills of northern England from Derbyshire to the Scottish border. Other long-distance routes include the South West Coast Path, the longest in England, the Wales Coast Path, which follows the entire Welsh coastline, the West Highland Way in Scotland and Offa's Dyke Path along the English-Welsh border. Walking is among the most popular recreational activities in Britain, supported by an extensive network of public footpaths and rights of way that cross private land. Accommodation along such routes ranges from campsites and bunkhouses to hotels and inns.

question: What is a public right of way in the British countryside?
option_a: A path the public may use to cross land, even where the land is privately owned
option_b: A track that may be used only with the owner's written permission
option_c: A route reserved for farm vehicles
option_d: A road maintained by the local council
explanation: Public rights of way are paths along which anyone may pass, including footpaths, bridleways and byways, and they frequently cross privately owned farmland, woods and estates. They are marked on Ordnance Survey maps and signposted on the ground, and landowners must keep them passable. Walkers are expected to follow the Countryside Code by keeping to paths where crops are growing, closing gates, controlling dogs near livestock and taking litter home. Legislation has also given a right to roam over designated areas of open country and common land in England and Wales, with broader access rights applying in Scotland. Councils keep a definitive map recording which paths carry public rights.

question: What does the Ordnance Survey produce?
option_a: Population statistics from the census
option_b: Weather forecasts for shipping
option_c: Records of historic buildings
option_d: Detailed maps of Great Britain
explanation: The Ordnance Survey is the national mapping agency for Great Britain, producing detailed paper and digital maps used by walkers, planners, emergency services and businesses. It originated in the eighteenth century in military surveys of the Scottish Highlands and of the south coast, which is the origin of the word ordnance in its name. Its familiar Landranger and Explorer series show footpaths, contours, field boundaries and landmarks in fine detail. The Met Office produces weather forecasts including the shipping forecast, and the Office for National Statistics conducts the census and publishes population data. Its maps use a national grid reference system that allows any point to be described precisely. Digital versions are now used by emergency services and by walking apps.

question: What is the shipping forecast?
option_a: A regular BBC radio broadcast of weather conditions in the seas around the British Isles
option_b: A television programme about the fishing industry
option_c: A government report on trade through British ports
option_d: A daily bulletin issued to airline pilots
explanation: The shipping forecast is broadcast several times a day on BBC Radio 4 and gives weather conditions and warnings for the sea areas surrounding the British Isles, read in a distinctive clipped format covering wind, weather, visibility and sea state. Names of the sea areas, such as Dogger, Fisher and German Bight, have become familiar to listeners far from the sea, and the broadcast is regarded with considerable affection as a piece of national background. It remains a genuine safety service for mariners, produced by the Met Office, which also issues severe weather warnings on land using a colour-coded system.

question: Which body produces official population and economic statistics for the UK?
option_a: The Bank of England
option_b: The Office for National Statistics
option_c: The Cabinet Office
option_d: The Electoral Commission
explanation: The Office for National Statistics is the United Kingdom's largest producer of official statistics, responsible for conducting the census in England and Wales and for publishing figures on population, births and deaths, migration, employment, earnings, inflation and economic output. Its statistics are produced independently of ministers and are used by government, businesses, researchers and journalists, and some, such as the inflation measure, directly affect pensions and benefits. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own statistical agencies conducting their censuses. The Bank of England sets interest rates, and the Electoral Commission oversees elections and party funding. Its figures are published to a pre-announced timetable to protect them from political interference.

question: What is the Met Office?
option_a: The UK's national weather service
option_b: A body regulating the metal industry
option_c: The headquarters of the Metropolitan Police
option_d: The office managing the national rail timetable
explanation: The Met Office is the national meteorological service of the United Kingdom, producing forecasts for the public, aviation, shipping, agriculture and the armed forces, and issuing severe weather warnings using a colour-coded system of yellow, amber and red. It also conducts climate research and runs some of the most powerful computers in the country to model the atmosphere. Storms affecting the United Kingdom and Ireland are given names from an annual list to help communicate risk clearly. The Metropolitan Police, often called the Met, is the police force for London, an entirely separate organisation. Its forecasts are broadcast several times a day on television and radio across the country. The service was founded in the nineteenth century, originally to help mariners.

question: How do most people in Britain travel to work?
option_a: Only by train
option_b: Almost entirely on foot
option_c: Mainly by domestic air travel
option_d: By car, with public transport widely used in larger cities
explanation: The car remains the most common way of travelling to work across the United Kingdom as a whole, although in London and other large cities a very high proportion of commuters use buses, trains, trams or the underground, and cycling and walking have grown in urban areas. Public transport is extensive in cities and much sparser in rural districts, where car ownership is close to essential. Working from home increased sharply during the coronavirus pandemic and has remained more common since. Congestion charging in London and clean air zones in several cities aim to reduce traffic and pollution. Season tickets and travelcards are widely used by regular commuters into cities.

question: What is the London Underground commonly called?
option_a: The Metro
option_b: The Overground
option_c: The Subway
option_d: The Tube
explanation: The London Underground, opened in 1863 and the oldest underground railway system in the world, is universally known as the Tube, a name derived from the circular tunnels of its deep-level lines. Its map, designed by Harry Beck in the 1930s on the principle of an electrical diagram rather than geographical accuracy, has been imitated by transit systems worldwide. Stations were used as air raid shelters during the Blitz. Other British cities have their own systems, including the Glasgow Subway, the Tyne and Wear Metro and tram networks in Manchester, Sheffield, Nottingham, Birmingham, Edinburgh and Croydon. Announcements warning passengers to mind the gap have become part of the city's character.

question: What is a distinctive feature of British roads compared with most of Europe?
option_a: Speed limits are measured in kilometres per hour
option_b: There are no motorways
option_c: All roads are toll roads
option_d: Traffic drives on the left
explanation: Vehicles in the United Kingdom drive on the left-hand side of the road, as they do in Ireland, Malta, Cyprus and many Commonwealth countries, whereas most of Europe and the Americas drive on the right. Distances and speed limits are given in miles and miles per hour rather than in kilometres, one of several areas in which imperial measures persist alongside the metric system. Roundabouts are used extensively in place of traffic lights at junctions. Motorways are toll-free with a very small number of exceptions, and driving requires a licence, insurance and, for older vehicles, a valid MOT test certificate.

question: What is an MOT test?
option_a: An annual roadworthiness and safety test required for most older vehicles
option_b: An inspection of a vehicle's insurance documents
option_c: A test of a driver's eyesight taken every five years
option_d: A qualification needed to drive a lorry
explanation: The MOT is an annual test of roadworthiness, safety and emissions that most vehicles over three years old must pass in order to be used on public roads. It checks items such as brakes, lights, tyres, steering, seat belts and exhaust emissions, and it is carried out at approved garages. Driving without a valid certificate is an offence and can invalidate insurance. Drivers must also hold a licence appropriate to the vehicle, have at least third-party insurance, and pay vehicle excise duty or register the vehicle as off the road. The name comes from the former Ministry of Transport. A vehicle that fails the test cannot be driven until the defects have been put right.

question: At what age can a person usually apply to learn to drive a car in the UK?
explanation: A person may usually apply for a provisional driving licence at sixteen but can begin learning to drive a car on public roads at seventeen, or earlier in some circumstances for those receiving certain disability benefits. Learners must display L plates, be accompanied by a qualified driver meeting age and experience requirements, and may not use motorways except with an approved instructor. Passing both a theory test, which includes hazard perception, and a practical driving test is required before driving unaccompanied. Mopeds of limited power may be ridden from sixteen. New drivers face losing their licence if they accumulate six penalty points within two years.

question: What is the Highway Code?
option_a: A map of the national road network
option_b: A law setting motorway speed limits only
option_c: A register of licensed drivers
option_d: The official guide to rules and good practice for road users
explanation: The Highway Code sets out the rules, advice and legal requirements for all road users in the United Kingdom, including drivers, motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders and pedestrians. Some of its provisions are legal requirements whose breach is an offence, while others are advisory but can be cited in court as evidence of whether someone drove carefully. It explains road signs and markings, stopping distances, the rules on roundabouts and crossings, and a hierarchy giving greater responsibility to those who can cause the most harm. Learner drivers study it for the theory test, and it is updated periodically. It applies across the United Kingdom, though a few details differ between the nations.

question: What must a driver in the UK have before driving on public roads?
option_a: Only a licence, as insurance is optional
option_b: A valid licence and at least third-party motor insurance
option_c: A permit from the local council
option_d: Membership of a motoring organisation
explanation: Anyone driving on public roads in the United Kingdom must hold a licence valid for the class of vehicle and must be covered by at least third-party motor insurance, which covers injury or damage caused to other people. Driving without insurance is a serious offence that can bring a fine, penalty points and disqualification, and the vehicle may be seized. Vehicles must also be taxed or declared off the road, and most over three years old need a valid MOT certificate. Drivers must wear seat belts, must not use a hand-held mobile phone, and must stay within the legal alcohol limit.

question: What happens if a driver accumulates too many penalty points?
option_a: Their insurance is paid by the government
option_b: They must retake the theory test but may keep driving
option_c: They can be disqualified from driving
option_d: They receive a warning letter only
explanation: Motoring offences such as speeding, using a hand-held phone while driving or careless driving usually result in penalty points being endorsed on the driver's licence, along with a fine. A driver who accumulates twelve points within three years is normally disqualified for a period by the court, and new drivers face a stricter limit of six points in their first two years, after which the licence is revoked and both tests must be taken again. Serious offences such as drink-driving or dangerous driving carry immediate disqualification and can result in imprisonment. Insurance premiums typically rise sharply after an endorsement. Courts may also order an extended retest before a licence is returned in serious cases.

question: Which of these is a UK-wide legal requirement in a car?
option_a: Displaying a national flag
option_b: Carrying a fire extinguisher
option_c: Carrying a spare set of bulbs
option_d: Wearing a seat belt where one is fitted
explanation: Drivers and passengers in the United Kingdom must wear a seat belt where one is fitted, with limited exemptions such as certain medical conditions and some delivery drivers travelling short distances. The driver is responsible for ensuring that children are properly restrained, using an appropriate child seat until the child reaches a specified height or age. Unlike in some European countries, there is no requirement to carry a fire extinguisher, warning triangle or spare bulbs, though many drivers do so. Using a hand-held mobile telephone while driving is prohibited and carries penalty points and a fine. Penalties apply to both the driver and, for adult passengers, to the individual not wearing a belt.

question: How is rail travel organised in Britain today?
option_a: A network operated by local councils
option_b: A national network with services run under contract and infrastructure managed centrally
option_c: A single state-owned company running everything
option_d: Entirely private railways with no regulation
explanation: Britain's railways were nationalised after the Second World War and privatised in the 1990s, and the present arrangement separates the track, signalling and stations, managed by a publicly owned infrastructure body, from passenger services, which are run by operators under contracts with government. Some services have returned to public control after operators failed. Fares, punctuality and investment are perennial subjects of complaint and political debate. The network carries very large numbers of commuters into London and other cities, and high-speed services connect London with Paris and Brussels through the Channel Tunnel. Ticket types range from advance fares booked ahead to flexible walk-up fares bought on the day. Railcards give discounts to young people, older travellers and families.

question: Which of these best describes the British attitude to animals as pets?
option_a: Pets must be licensed annually by the council
option_b: Keeping pets is discouraged by law
option_c: Only working animals may be kept
option_d: Pet ownership is very common, and animal welfare is protected by law
explanation: A large proportion of British households keep pets, most commonly dogs and cats but also rabbits, birds, fish and other animals, and the country has a long-standing reputation for attachment to them. The law requires owners to meet their animals' needs for a suitable environment, diet, companionship and protection from pain and suffering, and causing unnecessary suffering is a criminal offence that can lead to imprisonment and a ban on keeping animals. Dogs must be microchipped and wear an identifying collar in public. Charities including the RSPCA, the Dogs Trust and Battersea rescue and rehome very large numbers of animals each year.

question: How many members of Parliament sit in the House of Commons?
explanation: The House of Commons has 650 members, each elected to represent a geographical area known as a constituency. Members are chosen at a general election by the first past the post system, in which the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins the seat, and by-elections are held when a seat becomes vacant between general elections. The number of seats and their boundaries are reviewed periodically by independent boundary commissions to reflect changes in population. The Commons is the elected chamber and is the more powerful of the two houses, since the government must retain its confidence in order to remain in office.

question: What is a constituency?
option_a: The geographical area represented by a single member of Parliament
option_b: A department of the civil service
option_c: A committee of the House of Lords
option_d: A meeting of party members
explanation: A constituency is the area, with roughly comparable numbers of electors, that a single member of Parliament represents in the House of Commons. Voters in each constituency choose one member at a general election, and that member is expected to represent the interests of everyone living there, not only those who voted for them or who belong to their party. Members hold regular surgeries at which constituents can raise problems, and anyone may write to their member about a concern. Boundaries are reviewed periodically by independent commissions so that constituencies remain broadly equal in size as populations shift. Constituencies vary in area enormously, from a few square miles in cities to vast rural seats.

question: Which electoral system is used for UK general elections?
option_a: Proportional representation by party list
option_b: First past the post
option_c: The single transferable vote
option_d: The additional member system
explanation: General elections to the House of Commons use the first past the post system, under which the candidate receiving the most votes in each constituency is elected, even if that is less than half of the votes cast. The system tends to produce single-party majority governments and a strong link between a member and a particular area, but it can leave the national distribution of seats out of proportion to the votes cast. Other systems are used elsewhere in the United Kingdom: the Scottish Parliament uses an additional member system, the Senedd has been elected by a closed-list proportional system since 2026, and Northern Ireland uses the single transferable vote.

question: How often must a general election be held at the latest?
option_a: At least every five years
option_b: Every seven years
option_c: Only when the monarch decides
option_d: Every three years
explanation: A general election must be held at least every five years, and in practice a Prime Minister may seek an earlier dissolution of Parliament, in which case the monarch grants it on that advice. Elections are traditionally held on a Thursday. When a government loses the confidence of the House of Commons, an election commonly follows. After the election, the leader of the party able to command a majority is appointed Prime Minister by the monarch. Where no party wins an overall majority, the result is a hung parliament, which may lead to a coalition or to a minority government relying on support from others.

question: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
option_a: The House of Lords by a vote
option_b: The Speaker of the House of Commons
option_c: The electorate, who vote for the Prime Minister directly
option_d: The monarch, by convention choosing the person able to command a Commons majority
explanation: The monarch formally appoints the Prime Minister, but by long-standing convention the choice is not a personal one: the sovereign appoints whoever is best placed to command the confidence of the House of Commons, which is normally the leader of the party with the most seats. Voters do not vote for a Prime Minister directly; they elect a member of Parliament for their own constituency. This is why a change of party leader between elections can produce a new Prime Minister without a general election. The Prime Minister then appoints ministers, who are likewise formally appointed by the monarch on that advice.

question: What is the Cabinet?
option_a: The committee of senior ministers who take the most important government decisions
option_b: The staff of the Prime Minister's private office
option_c: The body that appoints judges
option_d: A committee of the House of Lords
explanation: The Cabinet is the group of around twenty senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister, most of whom head major government departments, and it meets weekly to take collective decisions on policy. Members are bound by collective responsibility, meaning that they must publicly support decisions once taken or else resign. Key posts include the Chancellor of the Exchequer, responsible for the economy and taxation, the Home Secretary, responsible for policing and immigration, the Foreign Secretary and the Secretaries of State for health, education and defence. Ministers are drawn from the House of Commons and the House of Lords and are accountable to Parliament.

question: Which minister is responsible for the economy and taxation?
option_a: The Foreign Secretary
option_b: The Lord Chancellor
option_c: The Home Secretary
option_d: The Chancellor of the Exchequer
explanation: The Chancellor of the Exchequer heads the Treasury and is responsible for the public finances, including taxation, government spending and economic policy, and delivers the annual Budget statement to the House of Commons. The Chancellor lives at 11 Downing Street, next door to the Prime Minister. The Home Secretary is responsible for policing, immigration, security and crime, the Foreign Secretary for international relations, and the Lord Chancellor, who is also usually the Justice Secretary, for the courts and the legal system. These offices, with the Prime Minister, are traditionally regarded as the most senior positions in government. The Chancellor traditionally holds up a red despatch box before delivering the Budget.

question: Which minister is responsible for policing and immigration?
option_a: The Defence Secretary
option_b: The Home Secretary
option_c: The Chancellor of the Exchequer
option_d: The Foreign Secretary
explanation: The Home Secretary heads the Home Office and is responsible for policing in England and Wales, national security and counter-terrorism, immigration, borders, citizenship and crime policy. Decisions about naturalisation and settlement, and the rules governing the Life in the UK test, fall within that department's remit. Policing and justice are devolved in Scotland and Northern Ireland, so the Home Secretary's writ does not run in those areas. The Foreign Secretary handles relations with other countries and consular services, the Defence Secretary the armed forces, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer taxation and public spending. The department also oversees the passport service and the issuing of visas. It is one of the largest and most demanding offices in government.

question: What is the role of the Speaker of the House of Commons?
option_a: To draft all new legislation
option_b: To advise the monarch on appointments
option_c: To lead the largest political party
option_d: To chair debates impartially and maintain order in the chamber
explanation: The Speaker presides over debates in the House of Commons, calls members to speak, rules on points of order and procedure, and can discipline members who break the rules of the House, including by ordering them to withdraw. Once elected by fellow members the Speaker gives up party allegiance entirely and must be seen to be impartial, and by convention the main parties do not campaign against the Speaker at a general election. The Speaker also represents the Commons in dealings with the Lords, the crown and outside bodies. Deputy Speakers share the work of chairing the House. The Speaker votes only to break a tie, and then according to established conventions.

question: What is the House of Lords?
option_a: The elected chamber of Parliament
option_b: A committee of the Cabinet
option_c: The second chamber of Parliament, which scrutinises and revises legislation
option_d: A court of appeal for criminal cases
explanation: The House of Lords is the second chamber of the United Kingdom Parliament. Its members are not elected: most are life peers appointed for their experience and expertise, and a group of Church of England bishops sit as the Lords Spiritual. The remaining hereditary peers lost the right to sit under an Act of 2026. The Lords examine and revise bills sent from the Commons, scrutinise the work of government and conduct inquiries through committees. They can delay legislation and ask the Commons to think again, but under the Parliament Acts they cannot ultimately block a bill the elected house is determined to pass, particularly in matters of taxation and spending.

question: How do most members of the House of Lords obtain their seats?
option_a: They are elected by the public
option_b: They inherit their seats in every case
option_c: They are appointed as life peers
option_d: They are chosen by the Speaker
explanation: The majority of members of the House of Lords are life peers, appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister, with some nominated by other party leaders and others recommended independently by the House of Lords Appointments Commission for their expertise in fields such as science, medicine, business, the armed forces or public service. A life peerage cannot be inherited. A limited number of hereditary peers retained seats after the reform of 1999 but lost them under an Act of 2026, and twenty-six senior Church of England bishops sit as the Lords Spiritual. Members who belong to no party sit as crossbenchers, which is unusual among second chambers internationally.

question: How does a bill become law in the UK?
option_a: It passes through both Houses of Parliament and receives royal assent
option_b: It is issued as an order by the Cabinet
option_c: It is signed by the Prime Minister alone
option_d: It is approved by a public referendum
explanation: A proposed law, known as a bill, is normally introduced in the House of Commons and goes through several stages: a first reading, a second reading with a debate on the principle, a committee stage at which it is examined line by line and amendments are considered, a report stage and a third reading. It then goes through comparable stages in the House of Lords, and any disagreements are resolved by passing the bill between the two houses. Once both agree, the bill receives royal assent from the monarch and becomes an Act of Parliament, though its provisions may come into force on a later date.

question: What is royal assent?
option_a: Permission from the monarch to hold an election
option_b: The monarch's power to veto any legislation at will
option_c: The monarch's formal approval that turns a bill into an Act of Parliament
option_d: A ceremony marking the opening of the legal year
explanation: Royal assent is the final stage in the passage of legislation, when the monarch formally approves a bill that both Houses of Parliament have passed, turning it into an Act. It is now a constitutional formality: no monarch has refused assent since the early eighteenth century, and the sovereign acts on the advice of ministers. The requirement nonetheless reflects the constitutional principle that laws are made by the Crown in Parliament. Similar arrangements apply to legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd and the Northern Ireland Assembly within their devolved competences. The formal words of assent are still recorded in Norman French, a survival from medieval practice. Once given, the Act is printed and published as law. Assent is announced to both Houses by their presiding officers.

question: What is the State Opening of Parliament?
option_a: A ceremony at which the monarch sets out the government's legislative programme
option_b: The election of the Speaker
option_c: The annual Budget statement
option_d: The first sitting of a new Cabinet
explanation: The State Opening of Parliament marks the beginning of a parliamentary session. The monarch travels in a state coach to the House of Lords and delivers a speech, written by the government, setting out the legislation ministers intend to bring forward. Members of the Commons are summoned to the Lords by an official known as Black Rod, whose knock on the closed door of the Commons chamber symbolises that house's independence from the crown. Debate on the contents of the speech follows over several days. The ceremony also includes a traditional search of the cellars, recalling the Gunpowder Plot of 1605.

question: What is the role of the monarch in the British system of government?
option_a: Head of state with ceremonial and formal duties, acting on ministers' advice
option_b: Head of government, taking day-to-day political decisions
option_c: The commander who decides military strategy
option_d: The chief judge of the Supreme Court
explanation: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy: the monarch is head of state but does not govern. The sovereign's functions include opening Parliament, giving royal assent to legislation, appointing the Prime Minister and other ministers, receiving foreign ambassadors and acting as a symbol of national continuity above party politics. These powers are exercised on the advice of ministers who are accountable to Parliament. The monarch is briefed on government business and meets the Prime Minister regularly, with the right, as one constitutional writer put it, to be consulted, to encourage and to warn, but not to overrule an elected government.

question: What is meant by parliamentary sovereignty?
option_a: Judges may strike down laws they consider unwise
option_b: Local councils can override national legislation
option_c: Parliament is the supreme law-making authority in the UK
option_d: The monarch may overrule any Act of Parliament
explanation: Parliamentary sovereignty is the principle that Parliament is the supreme legal authority in the United Kingdom, able to make or repeal any law, and that no Parliament can bind its successors. The courts apply and interpret legislation but cannot strike down an Act of Parliament as unconstitutional, unlike in countries with an entrenched written constitution. They can, however, rule that a minister or public body has acted beyond its legal powers, and under the Human Rights Act they may declare legislation incompatible with convention rights, leaving it to Parliament to decide what to do about it. The principle has been much debated in relation to devolution, referendums and international treaties.

question: What is the Opposition in Parliament?
option_a: The largest party not in government, which scrutinises and challenges ministers
option_b: Members of the House of Lords who oppose the monarch
option_c: A group of independent members with no party
option_d: The committee that examines public spending
explanation: The Opposition is formed by the largest party that is not in government, and its leader is formally titled the Leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition, a title expressing the idea that opposing the government of the day is a legitimate and necessary part of the constitution rather than disloyalty to the state. The Opposition appoints a shadow cabinet, with spokespeople assigned to challenge each government department, and it is given time in the parliamentary timetable to choose subjects for debate. Its central function is to hold ministers to account and to present an alternative government to the electorate. Its leader receives a salary for the role and has a seat on the front bench opposite the Prime Minister.

question: What happens at Prime Minister's Questions?
option_a: MPs question the Prime Minister in the Commons chamber each sitting Wednesday
option_b: Journalists interview the Prime Minister on television
option_c: The public submits written questions to Downing Street
option_d: The Prime Minister questions the Cabinet in private
explanation: Prime Minister's Questions is a weekly session in the House of Commons, normally held on Wednesdays when Parliament is sitting, at which members put questions to the Prime Minister. The Leader of the Opposition has a set number of questions and the exchanges are often noisy and adversarial, with the Speaker frequently calling for order. Backbench members from all parties also take part, often raising constituency matters. Other ministers answer questions on a rota for their own departments. The session is televised and broadcast and is one of the most visible forms of parliamentary accountability. The session lasts around half an hour and is one of the best attended events in the parliamentary week. Deputies stand in when the Prime Minister is abroad.

question: What are select committees?
option_a: Committees that draft all legislation
option_b: Panels that appoint senior judges
option_c: Meetings of party members to choose candidates
option_d: Cross-party groups of MPs or peers that examine the work of government departments
explanation: Select committees are groups of members, drawn from different parties in rough proportion to their strength in the House, which scrutinise the work, policy and spending of particular government departments or investigate broader subjects. They take evidence from ministers, officials, experts and members of the public, and publish reports to which the government must respond. Their hearings are usually held in public and often receive media attention. Chairs are elected by fellow members rather than appointed by party leaders, which has increased their independence, and the committees are regarded as one of the more effective checks on the executive. Both Houses operate committees, and those in the Lords often examine longer-term or cross-cutting questions.

question: What is the civil service?
option_a: Elected officials in local government
option_b: The staff employed directly by political parties
option_c: Members of the armed forces in administrative roles
option_d: Politically neutral officials who carry out government policy and advise ministers
explanation: The civil service consists of officials employed by government departments to advise ministers and to implement policy, and it is politically neutral and permanent, remaining in place when governments change. Civil servants are appointed on merit through open competition rather than by political patronage, and they are expected to serve whichever party is in office with equal commitment, offering honest advice in private and carrying out decisions loyally in public. Their core values are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Senior officials appear before parliamentary committees, although ministers remain constitutionally accountable to Parliament for their departments. Departments are led politically by ministers but managed day to day by a senior official known as a permanent secretary.

question: What is the role of party whips?
option_a: To chair debates in the House of Commons
option_b: To draft bills on behalf of the government
option_c: To organise their party's members in Parliament and encourage them to vote with the party
option_d: To appoint government ministers
explanation: Whips are members of Parliament appointed by their party to manage its business in the House, ensure that members attend important votes and persuade them to support the party line. The name comes from hunting, where a whipper-in kept the hounds together. Each week members receive a document, also called the whip, listing forthcoming business with underlining to show the importance of each vote, a three-line whip being the most insistent. Members who defy a strong whip may face sanctions, including in serious cases having the whip withdrawn, which means being expelled from the parliamentary party. Whips also arrange pairing, by which members on opposite sides agree to be absent together.

question: What is a backbencher?
option_a: A civil servant advising the Cabinet
option_b: A member of the House of Lords
option_c: An MP who is not a minister or a shadow minister
option_d: A candidate who lost an election
explanation: Backbenchers are members of Parliament who hold no ministerial or shadow ministerial office, and the name comes from their seats on the benches behind the front benches occupied by ministers and their opposition counterparts. They question ministers, serve on select committees and public bill committees, represent their constituents, and can introduce private members' bills, a small number of which become law each year. Because governments depend on their own backbenchers for votes, organised backbench opinion can have considerable influence over policy, and rebellions on the government side are carefully watched. A committee of backbench members helps decide which subjects are debated in their allotted time. Many ministers begin and end their careers on the back benches.

question: What is Hansard?
option_a: A committee examining public accounts
option_b: The library of the House of Commons
option_c: The official published record of debates in Parliament
option_d: The building where select committees meet
explanation: Hansard is the official report of proceedings in both Houses of Parliament, recording substantially what was said in debates along with the results of votes and written answers to questions. It takes its name from Thomas Hansard, an early printer of parliamentary reports. It is published promptly and is freely available online, so that anyone can read exactly what their representatives said and how they voted. Devolved legislatures publish equivalent records. Parliamentary proceedings are also televised and streamed, and the public may attend debates in the galleries or arrange a visit through their member of Parliament. Corrections are limited to obvious errors, so the record cannot be used to tidy up what was said.

question: How can a member of the public raise an issue with their MP?
option_a: By writing, emailing or attending a constituency surgery
option_b: By applying to the Speaker for permission
option_c: Only by petitioning the monarch
option_d: Only through a solicitor
explanation: Anyone may contact the member of Parliament for the constituency in which they live, whether or not they voted for them and regardless of whether they are entitled to vote at all. Members hold surgeries, usually at regular intervals in the constituency, where people can discuss problems in person, and they also receive letters and emails in large numbers. A member may take up a case with a government department, raise a matter in the House, or write to a minister. Members cannot intervene in the decisions of the courts, which are independent, nor in matters devolved to another legislature.

question: What is a petition to Parliament?
option_a: A legal action brought against the government
option_b: A formal request signed by members of the public, which may lead to a debate
option_c: A document appointing a new minister
option_d: A form used to register as a voter
explanation: Petitions allow members of the public to ask Parliament or the government to take action. Petitions can be submitted online through an official site, and those attracting a specified number of signatures receive a response from the government, while those passing a higher threshold are considered for debate in Parliament. Paper petitions can also be presented by a member of Parliament on behalf of constituents. The system gives citizens a direct means of raising concerns between elections, alongside writing to a member, joining a campaign group, taking part in lawful demonstrations and, most fundamentally, voting. Petitions must relate to something the government or Parliament is actually responsible for.

question: What is a pressure group?
option_a: An organisation that campaigns to influence government policy on particular issues
option_b: A group of civil servants advising ministers
option_c: A body that runs elections
option_d: A committee of the House of Lords
explanation: Pressure groups, sometimes called interest or campaigning groups, seek to influence public policy on particular questions without themselves seeking to form a government. They include environmental organisations, charities, trade associations, professional bodies, trade unions and campaigns on single issues, and they operate by lobbying ministers and members of Parliament, giving evidence to committees, publishing research, organising petitions and demonstrations and working through the media. Their activity is a normal and legitimate part of a democratic system, and there are rules requiring transparency about paid lobbying and about donations to political parties. Membership of such organisations is another way of taking part in public life between elections. Some groups have memberships larger than those of the political parties.

question: Which of these is a major political party in the UK?
option_a: The Republican Party
option_b: The Federalist Party
option_c: The Conservative Party
option_d: The Christian Democratic Union
explanation: The main political parties operating across Great Britain are the Conservative Party, the Labour Party and the Liberal Democrats, with the Green Party and Reform also contesting seats. Scotland and Wales have significant nationalist parties in the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru, while Northern Ireland has an entirely separate party system that includes the Democratic Unionist Party, Sinn Féin, the Alliance Party, the Ulster Unionist Party and the Social Democratic and Labour Party. Members of Parliament who belong to no party sit as independents. Anyone may join a political party, and parties select their own candidates for election. Party membership is open to anyone who supports the aims of the party and pays a subscription.

question: What is a hung parliament?
option_a: A parliament suspended by the monarch
option_b: A parliament that has been dissolved before an election
option_c: A parliament in which no single party has an overall majority of seats
option_d: A parliament in which the Speaker has resigned
explanation: A hung parliament occurs when no party wins more than half the seats in the House of Commons at a general election. The parties then negotiate, and the outcome may be a formal coalition, in which two or more parties govern together and share ministerial posts, or a minority government that relies on case-by-case support or on an agreement with a smaller party. A coalition between the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats governed from 2010 to 2015. First past the post usually produces majorities, so hung parliaments have been relatively rare, though they have occurred several times in recent decades. Talks between parties after such a result can take days, and the existing government remains in office meanwhile.

question: What is meant by 'the Crown' in a constitutional sense?
option_a: The jewels kept at the Tower of London
option_b: The Church of England's governing body
option_c: The state's executive authority, exercised by ministers in the monarch's name
option_d: The personal wealth of the royal family
explanation: In constitutional language the Crown means the institution of the state rather than the person of the monarch or the physical regalia. Prosecutions are brought in the name of the Crown, government departments act under Crown authority, civil servants are Crown servants, and ministers exercise certain prerogative powers on the Crown's behalf. This distinction explains phrases such as Crown Prosecution Service and Crown Court. The monarch personally retains only a small number of genuinely discretionary powers, exercising the rest on the advice of ministers who are answerable to Parliament and, through it, to the electorate. Crown land and Crown property are held by the state rather than owned personally by the monarch. Powers exercised in the Crown's name are known as the royal prerogative.

question: Where does the UK Parliament meet?
option_a: Downing Street
option_b: Buckingham Palace
option_c: The Palace of Westminster in London
option_d: Whitehall
explanation: The United Kingdom Parliament meets in the Palace of Westminster beside the Thames in central London, a building rebuilt in Gothic style by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin after fire destroyed most of the medieval palace in 1834. It contains the chambers of the House of Commons and the House of Lords, committee rooms, libraries and Westminster Hall, which survives from the eleventh century. The clock tower housing the bell known as Big Ben stands at its northern end. Downing Street contains the offices and residences of the Prime Minister and Chancellor, and Whitehall is the street where several government departments are located.

question: What is the significance of Westminster Hall?
option_a: It is the meeting place of the Supreme Court
option_b: It is the chamber where the Commons debates
option_c: It is the residence of the Speaker
option_d: It is the oldest part of the Palace of Westminster and has hosted trials and lyings-in-state
explanation: Westminster Hall dates from the end of the eleventh century and is the oldest surviving part of the Palace of Westminster, with a magnificent hammerbeam roof added in the fourteenth century. It housed the principal law courts of England for centuries and was the setting for historic trials, including those of Sir Thomas More and Charles I. Today it is used for ceremonial occasions, addresses by visiting heads of state, and the lying-in-state of monarchs, when the public files past the coffin. A separate chamber off the hall is used for additional Commons debates. Its roof, made of oak, is the largest medieval timber roof in northern Europe. The hall survived both the 1834 fire and wartime bombing.

question: What does it mean that the UK constitution is 'unwritten' or uncodified?
option_a: It is not contained in a single document but found in statutes, case law and conventions
option_b: No constitutional rules exist at all
option_c: It has never been changed since 1689
option_d: It exists only as an oral tradition
explanation: The United Kingdom has no single constitutional document. Its constitutional rules are found in Acts of Parliament such as the Bill of Rights, the Acts of Union, the Parliament Acts, the devolution statutes and the Human Rights Act; in decisions of the courts; in historic documents such as Magna Carta; and in conventions that are followed consistently though not legally enforceable, such as the convention that the monarch grants royal assent. Because constitutional rules can be changed by ordinary legislation, the arrangement is unusually flexible, which some regard as a strength and others as a weakness. Proposals for a codified constitution are periodically raised but have never been adopted.

question: What is a convention in the British constitution?
option_a: A rule set out in an Act of Parliament
option_b: A meeting of a political party's members
option_c: A treaty signed with another country
option_d: An established practice that is followed consistently although not legally enforceable
explanation: Constitutional conventions are practices that are consistently observed and regarded as binding in political terms, even though the courts will not enforce them. Examples include the convention that the monarch acts on ministerial advice, that the Prime Minister sits in the House of Commons, that ministers who lose the confidence of the House resign, and that the Lords do not block manifesto commitments of an elected government. Conventions allow the constitution to develop without formal amendment, but because they depend on self-restraint and shared understanding, disputes about whether a convention exists or has been broken can be difficult to resolve.

question: Which document of 1689 limited the powers of the monarch?
option_a: The Act of Union
option_b: Magna Carta
option_c: The Human Rights Act
option_d: The Bill of Rights
explanation: The Bill of Rights of 1689, passed after the Glorious Revolution, established that the monarch could not suspend or dispense with laws, levy taxes or maintain a standing army in peacetime without the consent of Parliament, and required frequent parliaments and free elections. It also guaranteed freedom of speech in parliamentary debate. Together with Magna Carta of 1215, which established that the ruler is subject to law, and the Act of Settlement of 1701, it forms part of the foundation of the British constitution. The Human Rights Act, passed in 1998, incorporated European Convention rights into domestic law. It was accepted by William and Mary as a condition of receiving the crown.

question: What are the two main functions of Parliament?
option_a: Deciding court cases and setting interest rates
option_b: Collecting taxes and commanding the armed forces
option_c: Running government departments and appointing judges
option_d: Making law and holding the government to account
explanation: Parliament's central functions are to make and amend law and to scrutinise the work of the government, questioning ministers, debating policy, examining spending and investigating issues through committees. It also approves taxation and public expenditure, and it debates matters of national importance. Government departments are run by ministers and civil servants rather than by Parliament itself, judges are appointed through an independent process, court cases are decided by the judiciary, and interest rates are set independently by the Bank of England. This separation of roles is central to how power is distributed in the British system. It also represents constituents, who can raise concerns with their own member at any time. Debates on petitions and emergency questions allow urgent matters to be aired.

question: What is the Budget?
option_a: The Chancellor's annual statement on taxation and public spending
option_b: The monarch's speech at the opening of Parliament
option_c: A report by the Bank of England on interest rates
option_d: The Prime Minister's list of ministerial appointments
explanation: The Budget is the statement delivered to the House of Commons by the Chancellor of the Exchequer setting out the government's plans for taxation and, alongside spending decisions, the management of the public finances. Changes to income tax, National Insurance, value added tax, duties on fuel, alcohol and tobacco, and allowances and thresholds are announced, and the measures then require the approval of Parliament through a Finance Bill. An independent body provides forecasts for the economy and the public finances alongside the statement. The requirement for parliamentary consent to taxation descends directly from the constitutional struggles of earlier centuries. Some announcements take effect immediately, while others begin at the start of the next tax year.

question: Who sets interest rates in the UK?
option_a: The House of Commons by vote
option_b: The Chancellor of the Exchequer directly
option_c: The Bank of England, independently of ministers
option_d: Commercial banks acting together
explanation: Since 1997 the Bank of England has set the official interest rate independently of government, through a Monetary Policy Committee that meets regularly and votes on whether to change the rate. Its objective is to keep inflation close to a target set by the government, currently expressed as an annual rate of two per cent, while supporting growth and employment. The arrangement was intended to remove short-term political considerations from monetary policy. The Bank is also responsible for issuing banknotes in England and Wales and, with other authorities, for the stability of the financial system. Minutes of the committee's meetings are published, showing how each member voted. The rate influences mortgage costs, savings returns and the value of the pound.

question: What is the National Audit Office responsible for?
option_a: Auditing the accounts of private companies
option_b: Collecting income tax from employers
option_c: Examining whether public money has been spent properly and effectively
option_d: Setting the annual Budget
explanation: The National Audit Office scrutinises public spending on behalf of Parliament, auditing the accounts of government departments and public bodies and reporting on whether money has been spent lawfully and has delivered value. Its reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons, a select committee traditionally chaired by a senior opposition member, which questions officials in public about failures and waste. Together they form an important element of financial accountability. Similar bodies operate in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to audit the spending of the devolved administrations. Its head, the Comptroller and Auditor General, is an officer of the House of Commons rather than a civil servant. Reports are published and are freely available to the public.

question: What is an Act of Parliament?
option_a: A law that has completed all parliamentary stages and received royal assent
option_b: A proposal for a law still being debated
option_c: A ruling by a senior court
option_d: A regulation issued by a government department
explanation: An Act of Parliament is legislation that has passed through both Houses and received royal assent, and it represents the highest form of law in the United Kingdom. Before it becomes an Act it is known as a bill. Acts often confer power on ministers to make more detailed rules, known as secondary or delegated legislation, which is subject to a lighter parliamentary procedure. Courts interpret and apply Acts but cannot set them aside, though they may quash secondary legislation that exceeds the powers granted by the parent Act. Acts remain in force until repealed or amended by Parliament. Each Act carries the year it was passed, which is how statutes are conventionally cited.

question: What is a private member's bill?
option_a: A bill introduced by an MP or peer who is not a government minister
option_b: A bill debated only in the House of Lords
option_c: A bill that applies only to one individual
option_d: Legislation drafted by the civil service
explanation: Private members' bills are introduced by backbench members of the Commons or by peers rather than by the government. Limited time is available for them, and most fail for want of time or government support, but a number have become law and some have brought about significant social change, including measures on abortion, the abolition of the death penalty and the decriminalisation of homosexual acts in the 1960s. Members are selected for priority by ballot at the start of a session. The government's own legislation, which occupies most of the parliamentary timetable, is known as public or government business. Supporters often need to gather enough members to prevent the bill being talked out.

question: What is a by-election?
option_a: An election for members of the House of Lords
option_b: A vote within a party to choose its leader
option_c: A general election called early by the Prime Minister
option_d: An election held in a single constituency when the seat becomes vacant
explanation: A by-election is held in one constituency between general elections when the sitting member dies, resigns, is disqualified or is removed through a recall petition. Only voters in that constituency take part, and the result does not change the government directly unless the parliamentary arithmetic is extremely tight. By-elections often attract national attention as a test of the government's popularity, and turnout is usually lower than at a general election. A member cannot simply resign, and the vacancy is created through an archaic procedure involving appointment to a nominal crown office. Campaigns are intense, with parties concentrating activists from across the country in one seat. Governing parties have historically tended to lose ground at them.

question: What is the Electoral Commission?
option_a: The body that counts votes in each constituency
option_b: A committee of the House of Commons
option_c: The office that draws constituency boundaries
option_d: An independent body overseeing elections, referendums and political finance
explanation: The Electoral Commission is an independent body that regulates political finance, registers political parties, reports on the conduct of elections and referendums, sets standards for those running them and promotes voter registration and participation. It publishes details of donations to parties and can investigate and sanction breaches of the rules. Votes are counted locally by returning officers appointed in each area, and constituency boundaries are set by separate independent boundary commissions. Together these arrangements are intended to ensure that elections are administered fairly and transparently and that public confidence in them is maintained. It also produces guidance for candidates on spending limits during a campaign. Breaches of the finance rules can result in fines and, in serious cases, prosecution.

question: Who is entitled to vote in a UK general election?
option_a: British, qualifying Commonwealth and Irish citizens aged 18 or over who are registered
option_b: Only people born in the United Kingdom
option_c: Only people who own property
option_d: Everyone resident in the UK regardless of nationality
explanation: To vote in a United Kingdom general election a person must be aged eighteen or over on polling day, be registered on the electoral roll, and be a British citizen, a qualifying Commonwealth citizen or a citizen of the Republic of Ireland resident in the country. Citizens of other countries, including those with settled status, cannot vote in general elections, although some may vote in local and devolved elections depending on where they live. Members of the House of Lords and convicted prisoners serving sentences are among those excluded. Registration can be completed online and is normally required by law when requested.

question: What must voters in Great Britain now bring to a polling station?
option_a: An accepted form of photographic identification
option_b: Their National Insurance card
option_c: A letter from their employer
option_d: Their birth certificate
explanation: Voters in Great Britain are now required to show an accepted form of photographic identification at a polling station before being given a ballot paper, following changes introduced in recent years. Accepted documents include a passport, a photocard driving licence, certain concessionary travel passes and a free voter authority certificate available to those without other identification. Photographic identification has been required in Northern Ireland for considerably longer. The change was intended to guard against personation, though critics argued that it risked deterring eligible voters, and its effects have been monitored by the Electoral Commission. Expired documents may still be accepted provided the photograph remains a good likeness. Postal voters are not affected by the requirement.

question: How can someone vote if they cannot attend a polling station?
option_a: They cannot vote at all
option_b: By voting online through a government website
option_c: By applying for a postal vote or appointing a proxy
option_d: By telephoning the returning officer on polling day
explanation: Electors who cannot attend in person may apply for a postal vote, which is sent to them in advance and returned by post or delivered to the polling station, or they may appoint a proxy, someone they trust who attends the polling station and votes on their behalf according to their instructions. Postal voting is available to any registered elector on request in Great Britain, and it is widely used by people who are away, working long hours or find travel difficult. Voting online is not available for parliamentary elections. Polling stations are open from early morning until late evening on polling day.

question: What is a manifesto?
option_a: A statement issued by the monarch at the state opening
option_b: The official record of parliamentary debates
option_c: A document setting out what a political party promises to do if elected
option_d: A list of registered voters
explanation: A manifesto is the document a political party publishes before an election setting out the policies it intends to pursue if it forms a government. Manifestos are scrutinised by journalists and opponents, and they matter constitutionally as well as politically: by convention the House of Lords does not block legislation that implements a commitment made in the winning party's manifesto, a practice known as the Salisbury convention. Parties are not legally bound to keep their promises, and circumstances may change, but failure to deliver on prominent commitments is a recurring subject of criticism and debate. Parties usually launch their manifestos at public events early in an election campaign.

question: What is the purpose of a referendum?
option_a: To put a specific question directly to the electorate for a decision
option_b: To appoint judges to the Supreme Court
option_c: To select a party leader
option_d: To choose members of Parliament
explanation: A referendum asks voters to decide a single question directly rather than choosing representatives. Referendums are not a regular feature of the British system, since the United Kingdom is a parliamentary democracy, but they have been used for major constitutional questions, including membership of the European Communities in 1975, devolution for Scotland and Wales, the Belfast Agreement in Northern Ireland, the voting system in 2011, Scottish independence in 2014 and European Union membership in 2016. Each requires its own Act of Parliament, which sets the question and the rules, and the Electoral Commission oversees the conduct of the poll. Results have sometimes been advisory in strict legal terms but treated as binding in practice.

question: Which body reviews the boundaries of parliamentary constituencies?
option_a: Independent boundary commissions
option_b: The Prime Minister's office
option_c: The Electoral Commission
option_d: The House of Lords
explanation: Separate independent boundary commissions for England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland review the boundaries of parliamentary constituencies periodically, so that the number of electors in each remains broadly equal as populations move and change. They consult publicly on their proposals before final recommendations are made. Keeping the process independent is intended to prevent the manipulation of boundaries for party advantage. The Electoral Commission has a different role, regulating political finance and overseeing the administration of elections, while returning officers in each area are responsible for running the poll and counting the votes. Reviews can be controversial, since changes to boundaries may favour one party over another. Their recommendations must be approved before taking effect.

question: What is meant by the separation of powers?
option_a: The division of the UK into four nations
option_b: The split between national and local taxation
option_c: The division of functions between Parliament, the government and the courts
option_d: The distinction between the Commons and the Lords
explanation: The separation of powers describes the division of the state's functions between the legislature, which makes law, the executive, which governs and implements it, and the judiciary, which interprets and applies it in individual cases. In the United Kingdom the separation is not complete, since ministers sit in Parliament rather than being kept separate from it, but judicial independence is strongly protected: judges cannot be dismissed at ministerial whim, they are appointed through an independent commission, and the Supreme Court was created in 2009 to move the highest court out of the House of Lords and make that independence visible.

question: What is the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom?
option_a: The court that tries the most serious criminal cases at first instance
option_b: A committee of the House of Lords
option_c: The highest court of appeal for civil cases throughout the UK and for criminal cases outside Scotland
option_d: The court that hears all cases involving the monarch
explanation: The Supreme Court, established in 2009 and sitting opposite the Houses of Parliament in Parliament Square, is the final court of appeal for civil cases from all parts of the United Kingdom and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Criminal appeals from Scotland end in the High Court of Justiciary in Edinburgh. It hears cases of the greatest public or constitutional importance, including disputes about the powers of government and about devolution. Its creation transferred the judicial role of the House of Lords to a separate institution, making the independence of the judiciary clearer. Its justices do not wear wigs or robes when hearing cases, unlike judges in many other courts.

question: What are members of the Scottish Parliament called?
option_a: MPs
option_b: Senators
option_c: MSPs
option_d: MLAs
explanation: Members of the Scottish Parliament are known as MSPs. There are 129 of them, elected by an additional member system in which each voter casts one ballot for a constituency member and another for a regional list, producing a result that is more proportional than first past the post. The Parliament sits at Holyrood in Edinburgh and legislates on devolved matters including health, education, justice, policing, housing, the environment and aspects of taxation. Members of the United Kingdom Parliament are called MPs, members of the Northern Ireland Assembly are MLAs, and members of the Senedd in Wales are known as MSs.

question: What are members of the Northern Ireland Assembly called?
option_a: MLAs
option_b: MEPs
option_c: MSs
option_d: MSPs
explanation: Members of the Northern Ireland Assembly are known as MLAs, standing for Members of the Legislative Assembly. They are elected by the single transferable vote, a form of proportional representation in which voters rank candidates in order of preference and several members are returned for each constituency. The Assembly sits at Stormont near Belfast and operates on a power-sharing basis so that both unionist and nationalist communities take part in government, with the First Minister and deputy First Minister holding equal authority. Key decisions may require cross-community support, a safeguard built into the Belfast Agreement of 1998. The Assembly has ninety members, with several returned from each constituency.

question: Who leads the devolved government in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland?
option_a: The First Minister
option_b: The Lord Lieutenant
option_c: The Prime Minister
option_d: The Secretary of State
explanation: Each devolved administration is led by a First Minister, who heads the executive and appoints ministers to run departments in the same way that the Prime Minister appoints the Cabinet at Westminster. In Northern Ireland the arrangement is distinctive: a First Minister and a deputy First Minister are appointed from the two largest designations and hold equal powers, so neither can act without the other. The Prime Minister leads the United Kingdom government, and a Secretary of State for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland represents the interests of each nation within that government and handles matters that remain reserved. Each First Minister is nominated by their own legislature after an election.

question: Which of these is a reserved matter, decided by the UK Parliament rather than a devolved body?
option_a: Defence and foreign policy
option_b: Schools in Wales
option_c: The National Health Service in Scotland
option_d: Housing in Northern Ireland
